en: The Laws of Manu,
together with the commentary composed by Medhātithi:
Having approached Manu as he sat with a concentrated mind, the great seers [spoke].
Having honored him according to custom, they spoke these words. || 1.1 ||
Salutation to the Supreme Brahman, who is the reality to be known through the Vedānta, who is the cause of the three worlds, and in whom all defects have been utterly destroyed. || 1 ||

By means of these four verses, the author establishes the preeminence of this treatise as well as its status as a teacher of human goals that cannot be known through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for the sake of its firm foundation. For when a treatise is firmly established by its authors, they attain heaven and fame, which remain with them as long as the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) lasts. Furthermore, a treatise gains a firm foundation only if certain individuals engage in its study, hearing, reflection, and so forth. And those who act with deliberate intelligence ought not to engage in study and the like without having ascertained the purpose. Therefore, the Teacher recited these four verses in order to demonstrate: "This treatise is commenced for the sake of thoroughly knowing the means for the accomplishment of human goals."

Nor should it be argued: "Even without stating the purpose at the outset, we shall arrive at this conclusion simply by reflecting upon the sequence of the treatise as it is about to be expounded; what is the need for such an effort to establish it? Furthermore, even if the purpose has been stated, it is not definitively ascertained until it is subsequently examined. For not all human utterances serve as a cause for certainty regarding their meaning. Nor is there a rule that engagement [with a work] must always be preceded by a full knowledge of its purpose, since we observe engagement in the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) and the like, which does not depend on such a motive. Even among human compositions, the statement of the purpose is not observed in every case. For instance, the venerable Pāṇini begins his collection of aphorisms with "Now begins the instruction of words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*) without having stated the purpose at all.

To this it is replied: If the purpose were not determined at the outset, people would certainly not take up the book at first; and because they do not take it up, how could they examine the treatise in its entirety? Furthermore, that very meaning which emerges as an object of the intellect through an examination of the beginning and the end becomes easy to grasp when stated briefly at the outset. As it has been said: "For in this world, the wise desire to hold both the concise and the detailed."

As for the objection: "Even though it has been stated, it is not ascertained because there is no ascertainment of the meaning from human-authored statements. One may have the cognition that 'this person knows this very thing,' but the object itself is not thus [ascertained]. We do not dispute here whether such ascertainment exists or does not exist, for that would lead to an excessive prolixity of the text. Even when there is doubt regarding the subject matter, activity is established; however, the arising of a doubt concerning a specific object cannot occur without a statement of the purpose (*prayojana*). For if it were not stated, one might also doubt: "Is this a treatise on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*), or a treatise on worldly affairs (*arthaśāstra*), or perhaps something like an examination of a crow's teeth? But when the purpose is declared, activity is established through the thought: "He tells us this much: 'I shall show you the path to the highest good. There is no harm to me in engaging with this. Very well, I shall investigate it. Thus, activity is accomplished.

However, the engagement in the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) belongs to one who is impelled by a teacher, not through the realization of his own entitlement (*adhikāra*). For at that time, due to childhood, he is not capable of realizing his own entitlement; rather, the accomplishment of engagement occurs solely through the prompting of another. Furthermore, it is not even made known by the presentation of an entitlement. Therefore, for one engaged therein, the purpose is the comprehension of the meaning, and from that arises the engagement. But here [in the case of the Smṛti rule]: "That twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in another [activity]... (MDh 2.168).

Thus ends the section on the qualification for study by one who has mastered the Veda. At that stage, because his intellect is fully developed, he seeks the purpose [of the treatise]. Furthermore, the sūtras of the venerable Pāṇini are extremely concise; there is no suspicion that they might intend to express some other meaning. In that regard, since Pāṇini’s fame is renowned even among children, his purpose is so well-known that it need not be stated. However, this extensive work is rich in various explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) and is useful for all human goals. Therefore, in stating the purpose for the sake of easy comprehension, nothing is lost.

And there are two types of practitioners: those who rely on reason (*nyāya*) and those who rely on established tradition (*prasiddhi*). Regarding the latter, it is said: "Whatever Manu declared is indeed medicine" (MS 2.1.5).
Furthermore: "The *ṛg*, *yajus*, and *sāman* verses, the mantras of the Atharvans, and whatever was proclaimed by the Seven Seers—all that Manu has spoken."

The meaning of this is as follows: because its power is renowned in the world through such explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), histories (*itihāsa*), and Purāṇas—or because it is established by the very fact of that renown—that this [work] was composed by Prajāpati, whose authority is determined by the fall of his matted locks; and it is for this reason alone that those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) engage with it. For them, even the connection with a specific author is a factor in their engagement. For this very reason, the statement of the purpose is presented in the form of a question and answer: the great sages (*maharṣi*) are the questioners and Prajāpati is the speaker. Furthermore, the subject matter—the definition of Dharma—is not something to be understood from common worldly experience, but is the exclusive domain of scripture, wherein even the great sages are in doubt; such is the intent of the injunction. Also, there is the point that he was questioned by them, yet he says "I was not questioned," as well as the fact that he is an uncreated image of Brahmā himself, and so forth. Thus, the purport of these four verses is that the commencement of the treatise is justified for the sake of explaining that [Dharma].
And just as it is stated that this treatise has the human goal as its primary purpose, we shall demonstrate that through the interpretation of the meaning of the words.

In that context, the great sages, having approached Manu, spoke these words: “It behoves you to declare the dharmas to us” (MDh 1.2). Being thus questioned, he replied: “Let it be heard” (MDh 1.4). In this way, the question and the answer both have as their primary purport the elucidation of a single subject matter. Therefore, it is effectively stated that the dharmas are what are to be expounded here. Furthermore, in common usage, the word *dharma* is employed to denote the means of attaining the highest good (*śreyas*), provided that such means are not established by worldly means of knowledge other than verbal testimony, such as perception. Consequently, by the connection with the phrase “let it be heard,” it is stated that [the dharmas] are the means for achieving the specific goals of human existence.

A certain distinguished person named Manu, endowed with the study, knowledge, and practice of numerous Vedic branches, and renowned through a tradition of successive memory (smṛti), was approached. "Approaching" means going into his presence directly, having abandoned other activities, and not meeting him by mere chance. By this effort of approaching, both the importance of the matter being inquired about and the authority of the speaker are made manifest; for those who are unskilled in giving answers do not come and inquire with such diligent effort.

"He was sitting with one-pointed attention, standing with one-pointed attention, and being with one-pointed attention. Here, "sitting" (*āsana*) does not refer to the act of sitting on a grass mat or similar seat, as that would be irrelevant; rather, by "sitting," a state of composure is indicated. One who is in such a state becomes capable of responding. Regarding the word "having approached" (*abhigamya*), Manu alone is the object of the action. However, for the act of questioning, "sitting with one-pointed attention" serves as a qualification. Having perceived him to be one-pointed—meaning his mind was undistracted—and attentive to hearing the question through the engagement in conversation appropriate to a greeting of well-being, he spoke these words.

The word *ekāgra* denotes immobility by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). For one whose mind has been freed from the contact with defects such as passion through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), stability of the mind during reflection on the realization of reality—the cessation of conceptual construction—is *ekāgratā*. Only when the mind is in such a state is it capable of discerning proximate objects such as forms and sounds, and not when it is joined with constructions of existence or non-existence. Alternatively, the word *agra* refers to the mind by virtue of its connection (*yoga*), because it moves ahead of the eyes and other senses in the apprehension of an object. In common parlance, that which is endowed with the first activity and is foremost is called "the front" (*agra*). The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a single [object]—be it the meditative object (*dhyeya*) or the object to be grasped (*grāhya*)—as its front. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound even though the members have different grammatical referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*), because the meaning is clear. Here too, the cessation of distraction is precisely what constitutes *ekāgratā*.

"Having honored according to the rule": *nyāya* is the boundary prescribed by the scriptures. Without transgressing that—having honored in the manner prescribed by the scripture for the first approach to a guru, such as salutation, attendance, and so forth—and having demonstrated devotion and respect.

The great seers (*maharṣis*). A seer (*ṛṣi*) is the Veda; the term "seer" is also applied to a person due to their excellence in the study, understanding, and practice of its meaning. They are both "great" and "seers. They become "great" through the ultimate excellence of those very same qualities, just as it is said, "Yudhiṣṭhira is the most excellent of the Kurus. Alternatively, they are "great" because of their specific asceticism (*tapas*) or because of their specific honor and renown.

They "spoke this speech" (*idaṃ vacanam abruvan*). "Speech" (*vacanam*) is that by which something is spoken; it refers to the sentence of the question in the second verse that is about to be stated. Because it is proximate, he points back to it with the word "this" (*idam*). Even for those who hold that the word "this" (*idaṃśabdaḥ*) indicates a perceptible object, the question is nonetheless perceptible because it resides in the mind. Alternatively, "speech" (*vacanam*) is that which is being spoken—the thing being asked about—and thus, on the view that it is a sentence, they "uttered this sentence. However, if the word "speech" (*vacana*) is derived as the object (*karman*), then "they asked this. In that case, the verb *brū* takes two objects; Manu is the "unexpressed object" (*akathitakarman*), while he is the object of the three actions [of speaking, asking, and uttering]. (1.1)
In response to the expectation of what they said after approaching and honoring him, the second verse follows:
"O Blessed One, you ought to tell us the duties (*dharma*) of all the social classes (*varṇas*) in their proper order, as well as those born from intermediate castes (*antaraprabhava*). (1.2)

The word *bhaga* refers to sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), magnanimity (*audārya*), fame (*yaśas*), and valor (*vīrya*). One who possesses these is a *bhagavat*. Thus, the address is "O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*). Furthermore, the term *varṇa* applies to the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of including the Śūdra; otherwise, since the questioners were great sages (*maharṣi*), the inquiry would have been restricted to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). The "intermediate" (*antara*) refers to that which lies between them. Due to the intermixture (*saṃkara*) of two castes, there arises a single caste that is incomplete. Those whose origin or birth (*prabhava*) is in the intermediate space are the "intermediate-born" (*antaraprabhava*), such as the *anuloma* and *pratiloma* offspring: the *Mūrdhāvasikta*, *Ambaṣṭha*, *Kṣattṛ*, *Vaidehika*, and so forth. Indeed, it is not appropriate to designate them by the caste of either the mother or the father alone. Just as a donkey born from the union of a donkey and a horse is neither a donkey nor a horse, but a distinct species altogether, so too are these intermediate-born individuals. Therefore, because they are not included under the term "caste" (*varṇa*), they are mentioned separately.

Is it not the case that those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) are held to belong to their mother’s caste? We say: no. For they are said to be merely "similar" (*sadṛśa*) to their mother’s caste; they are similar to that caste, but not of that caste itself. Furthermore, this status of theirs is based on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), not established by the inherent nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*). Therefore, because they fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when they are included within the category of those possessing *dharma*, they are indeed eligible for the instruction of the treatise. Moreover, virtues such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) will be taught even for those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*). As for the statement that they are "devoid of *dharma*," that is intended to mean the absence of specific duties such as vows (*vrata*) and fasts (*upavāsa*). By this, the utility of the treatise for all persons is demonstrated.

"Yathāvat" means "in accordance with what is appropriate. The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of "deserving" (*arhati*). In whatever manner a performance is appropriate—whether it be that this is obligatory (*nitya*), this is optional (*kāmya*), this is a subsidiary (*aṅga*), or this is the primary (*pradhāna*)—as well as the regulations concerning the substance, place, time, agent, and so forth, such is the scope of the term "appropriate" (*arhati*).

"In successive order" (*anupūrvaśaḥ*). "Successive order" (*ānupūrvī*) means sequence. Let that sequence by which [the rites] are to be performed also be stated: "After the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the tonsure (*cauḍa*) and the tying of the girdle (*mauñjīnibandhana*)," and so forth. By the word "properly" (*yathāvat*), completeness regarding the constituent elements (*padārtha*) is expressed; however, since sequence is not itself a constituent element, "in successive order" is mentioned separately.

The word *dharma* is used in the sense of injunction (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, as well as in reference to the action directed toward those [injunctions and prohibitions] for the sake of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). However, this inquiry—whether both are its primary meaning or whether one is secondary—is not undertaken here, because it has been treated at length in other texts and is of no use in the present context. In any case, in such instances as "the Aṣṭakās are to be performed" and "one should not eat *kalañja*," an obligation (*kartavyatā*) regarding the Aṣṭakās is understood, and a prohibition regarding the eating of *kalañja*. Thus, whether the ritual act called the Aṣṭakā is *dharma*, or whether the obligation directed toward it is *dharma*, there is no difference in the result. Furthermore, from the teaching of the nature of *dharma*, it follows by implication that whatever is contrary to it is *adharma*. Therefore, it is stated that both *dharma* and *adharma* are the subject matter of the scripture. In that regard, the performance of the Aṣṭakās is *dharma*, and the avoidance of killing a Brahmin and so forth is also *dharma*; the non-performance of the Aṣṭakās is *adharma*, and the commission of killing a Brahmin and so forth is *adharma*. This is the distinction between *dharma* and *adharma*.

By the term "arhasi" (you ought), they indicate the teacher's qualification for the exposition through the fitness characterized by capability. Since you are capable of speaking the Dharmas, therefore, being authorized, you shall be requested [to speak] with the words "speak. The word of request, "speak," which is understood through implication—that whatever one is authorized to do must be performed by him—is supplied [as an ellipsis]. 1.2.

It has been stated that the word *dharma* applies to the mere activity (*vyāpāra*) directed toward an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). In this regard, just as it is used in connection with the Aṣṭaka and other such rites, so too is it used in connection with the worship of the *caitya* and the like. Since a doubt may arise as to which specific *dharmas* are intended here, the verse beginning with “You alone” (*tvam ekaḥ*) is spoken for the purpose of explaining those specific *dharmas* and to establish the capacity [of the Lord] already mentioned:
“For You alone, O Lord, are the knower of the true meaning of the effects of this entire self-existent ordinance—which is inconceivable and immeasurable. (1.3)

You alone are one, without companion, without a second. You are the knower of the true meaning and purpose of the entire *vidhāna*—that is, the scripture (*śāstra*), so called because by it actions are enjoined. This refers to the Veda, known as the self-existent (*svayaṃbhū*), eternal, uncreated, and not of human origin. It includes everything, both that whose syllables are directly perceptible and that whose syllables are to be inferred. For example, in the case of the direct statement: "One should offer the *agnihotra*; with this [verse], 'This thousandfold man,' he worships the *āhavanīya* fire," the Veda itself directly enjoins the oblation. Furthermore, by the instrumental case in the word "with this" (*etayā*), the application of the directly perceptible mantra for the worship of the *āhavanīya* is made manifest. In the case of the injunction "The *Aṣṭakā* rites should be performed," however, the Veda is inferred through tradition (*smṛti*). From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra "I cut the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) which is the seat of the altar," there is an inference of the scriptural text (*śruti*) "He cuts the sacrificial grass with this. For this mantra is recited in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and the cutting of the sacrificial grass is prescribed therein. While the specific rule "one should cut with this mantra" does not exist, the mantra is by its very form capable of manifesting the cutting of the sacrificial grass. Its connection to the New and Full Moon sacrifices is established generally through the context; yet, by its own capacity, it is employed in the cutting of the grass. Such is the understanding here: due to the context, one should perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices with this mantra. How? By whatever means possible; for even though not explicitly stated, capacity (*śakti*) is a universal auxiliary factor. What, then, can the mantra do? It can manifest the cutting of the sacrificial grass. Thus, from the context and its own capacity, the verbal expression "he cuts the sacrificial grass" arises in the mind. Since words are first perceived through conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*), that word residing in the intellect is called the "inferred Veda" (*anumeya-veda*). And its status as Veda is established because it is raised up by its own capacity from the two other scriptural texts—the prose injunction of the New and Full Moon sacrifices and the mantra-text itself. This is the position of Kumārila.

Alternatively, *vidhi* (injunction) means prescription, performance, or the accomplishment of a purpose. This pertains to everything belonging to the Self-Existent (*svayaṃbhū*), which is eternal and handed down through an unbeginning tradition, whether it is expounded by the Self-Existent or by the Veda—whether it is expressed by the syllables actually heard or understood through the power of the meaning already grasped. For Vedic injunction is of two kinds: some is directly expressed by words; for example, in the text "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer the *caru* oblation to Sūrya," the person desiring spiritual luster is qualified for the *saurī caru*. It is understood that this procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for accomplishing spiritual luster through that *caru* is like that of the *āgneya* sacrifice. In both cases, this cognition is indeed verbal, because its root lies in the comprehension of words. Both are understood from the word: one through direct denotation (*abhidhāna*), and the other through the understanding of what is denoted (*abhidheya*). However, a distinction caused by mediation and so forth does not negate its verbal nature. Just as water in a well, struck by the hand, strikes another spot, yet that too is struck precisely through the contact with the striker, though not directly; or as in the upward movement of pebbles, their successive leaps and falls are produced solely by the initial effort. Such is this case: in a modified ritual (*vaikṛta-karman*), there is a connection with a specific procedure. Thus, in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," since an originative injunction cannot be devoid of a qualification, the understanding of the qualification "one desiring heaven" is reached through the power of the meaning already grasped. Therefore, the term "of all" (*sarvasya*) in the phrase "the prescription of all" indicates that the purport (*tātparya*) of everything is of this nature, namely, that the Smṛtis have the Veda as their source. We shall demonstrate this in the second [chapter].

But surely, the meaning conveyed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers is an injunction (*vidhi*) consisting of the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*), and that is everywhere expressed solely by a perceptible word. In that case, why is it said that "Vedic injunction is of two kinds"? [The answer is: From the expression "one should offer" (*nirvapet*), the *kartavyatā* (the state of being to be done) is understood; however, the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is understood through the force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*), in the manner already described.

This is not a fault. When it is understood that "one should offer" (*nirvapet*) or "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the duty to be performed (*kartavyatā*) is not fully realized merely through the object of the verbal root's meaning. Rather, it remains incomplete as long as the other constituent parts—namely, the qualification (*adhikāra*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and the performance (*prayoga*)—are not understood. It is through these parts that the injunction (*vidhi*) is perceived in its expanded form. Therefore, even these constituent parts are not contradictory to being expressed by the word "injunction" (*vidhi*).

He says this very thing: “of the inconceivable” (*acintyasya*). This means “of that which is not perceptible” (*apratyakṣasya*). For what is perceptible is said to be experienced; it is not thought of, nor is it remembered. [The Veda is] “immeasurable” (*aprameyasya*), meaning it is to be inferred and is generally based on the authority of traditional memory (*smṛti-vākya*). Indeed, it is not measured by direct perception. Therefore, it is called “immeasurable. Alternatively, it is “immeasurable” because its magnitude cannot be determined due to its extreme vastness. The Veda, divided into many different branches, cannot be measured by everyone. For this very reason, it is “inconceivable. That which is exceedingly great is called “inconceivable” because it is difficult to grasp. Just as people say in the world, “What is the fate of others? Even to think about this is not appropriate,” so too, while the mind is said to have all things as its object, this [Veda], because of its extreme vastness, is not even an object for it. By these two words, the Teacher encourages [the listener] by proclaiming its greatness through its being the object of both external and internal organs: “By you alone has such a Veda been brought forth; therefore, you know—that is, you understand—the true meaning of it in its form as action (*kārya-rūpa-tattvārtha*).”

That which is to be performed is called *kārya*. It is that wherein a person is enjoined as an agent: "This must be done by you," or "This must not be done by you"; for example, the *agnihotra* and other such rites are to be performed, while the eating of *kalañja* (poisonous mushrooms) and the like are not to be performed. Even a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) is indeed a performance. That very non-performance of killing a Brāhmaṇa is itself the performance of the prohibition. Both engagement (*pravṛtti*) is an action (*kriyā*), and cessation (*nivṛtti*) is also an action. For it is not only that which is accomplished through the means of physical movement that is called "performance. What then? Even the cessation of an activity when its form has presented itself is [a performance]. As in the case of the saying, "One who consumes what is beneficial lives long": he who eats when it is the proper time and does not eat when it is not, even his abstaining from food is indeed beneficial.

Alternatively, the word *kārya* (what is to be done) is used for the sake of illustration, representing both injunction (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). Only this much constitutes the essential, ultimate meaning of the Veda. However, that which consists of the description of past events—such as, "He wept; because he wept, that is the Rudra-nature of Rudra" (TS 1.5.1.1; Nir 10.5)—is not the essential meaning. This is because such passages form a single syntactical unit with another injunction, and, being intent on praise, they lack any finality regarding their own literal sense. For there exists another injunction here: "Therefore, silver must not be given upon the sacrificial grass" (TS 1.5.1.2). Passages beginning with "He wept" and ending with "there will be weeping in his house before a year has passed" (TS 1.5.1.1–2) form a single syntactical unit with that [injunction]; by censuring the giving of silver upon the sacrificial grass, they praise its prohibition. Thus it has been said: "The Veda is an authority regarding what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), not regarding what is already established (*siddharūpa*). For the meaning of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is of an established nature. Indeed, no obligation to act is perceived from their meaning; rather, they are perceived to be subordinate to the instruction of an injunction. If they were also intent on their own literal sense, then their subordination to injunction would be contradicted. Consequently, the perceived unity of the sentence would be sublated. And when a unity of sentence is possible, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is not logical. Furthermore, a unity of sentence cannot be achieved by making something to be accomplished dependent on an established fact. For in that case, nothing at all would be taught by the Veda as something to be performed; thus, the Veda would become non-authoritative. Moreover, the status of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth as having the sense of an injunction would be abandoned. Therefore, the blessed Manu stated that the essential meaning of the Veda is of the nature of what is to be done (*kāryarūpa*). Jaimini also stated that the Veda is an authority regarding what is to be done: "Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction" (PMS 1.1.2).

And thus, because he possesses the excellence of complete knowledge regarding all things without exception, the capacity for proclaiming the Dharma is established as a matter of fact; hence the address "O Lord. [The request is: "O Lord, you who are capable of declaring the Dharma, please explain the Dharmas. Having been thus questioned about the Dharmas by these three verses, he gave his promise with the following verse. 1.3.
Thus questioned by those high-souled ones, Amitaujas duly honored all those great seers and replied, "Listen. 1.4.

That Manu, possessed of immeasurable power (*amitaujas*), being thus questioned by those great-souled great seers (*maharṣis*), replied to them, saying, "Listen. The word *tathā* (thus) refers to the manner previously mentioned. Both the subject matter to be asked about and the method of questioning are included within the word *tathā*. Therefore, the meaning is: having been questioned in that manner—having been questioned regarding those duties—he replied. Alternatively, *tathā* indicates the mere manner; since the specific object of the question is already present in the mind from the preceding verse due to the word "questioned," the fact that the question and the reply share the same object is established by the phrase "what he was asked, that he replied, saying 'Listen'. In that case, the word *tathā* serves merely to complete the verse. In the first explanation, however, the shared object of the question and the reply is precisely what is conveyed by the word *tathā*. The word *samyak* (properly) is an adjective qualifying the reply. He replied properly—that is, with a tranquil mind and not through the influence of anger or other such emotions. "Of immeasurable power" means one whose capacity for speech is undiminished; that is, he possesses immeasurable (*amita*) and infinite (*ananta*) vigor (*ojas*) or prowess, namely the power of expression. He states "the great seers" to show that there is no contradiction between their status as great seers and their role as questioners of Dharma, given their greatness of soul. A "great-souled one" (*mahātman*) is defined as "one who constantly acts for the sake of others. Therefore, although they were themselves wise and had realized the truth as it is—otherwise their status as great seers would be untenable—they nevertheless questioned [Manu] for the sake of others. Manu is of a most renowned authority; what he says is respected by the world. Because he is honored on account of his credibility, we appoint him as our teacher for the purpose of introducing this scripture. And being questioned by us, he will be regarded as even more authoritative by the people. For this very reason, the act of honoring them all is not contradictory; otherwise, what kind of honor could a disciple show to a teacher? The form *ārcya* is the gerund (*lyabanta*) of the root *arc* preceded by the prefix *ā*. An alternative reading is "having honored them" (*arcayitvā tān*).

Regarding this, it is said: if this work was composed by Manu himself, then it is not appropriate for him to speak in the third person, saying, "Being questioned by them, he replied"; rather, it would have been proper for him to say, "Being questioned, I replied. Alternatively, if someone else were the author of the work, how is it that it bears the designation "of Manu" (Mānava)?

That is not to be questioned. Generally, authors state their own views under the guise of another, saying, "On this point he says," or "On this point they reply," rather than saying, "I was asked by them. Whosoever is earlier is accepted by the world as more authoritative, as in the statement: "That is the authority of Bādarāyaṇa. Alternatively, this *saṃhitā* was proclaimed by Bhṛgu, but because it is composed in the form of a *smṛti* (traditional law) of Manu, it bears the designation "of Manu. He replied to those great sages: what was that? Listen to that which I was asked. (1.4)
In the beginning, this was enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without distinguishing marks, beyond the reach of reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely asleep. (1.5)

Where have they gone? Where have they fallen? Having been asked about the principles of falling as stated in the scriptures and having promised to explain those very things, [the author] instead provides a description of the indeterminate state (*avyākṛtāvasthā*) of the world; this is irrelevant and does not serve any human purpose (*apuruṣārtha*). This is the well-known popular saying: "Being asked about mangoes, he speaks of *kovidāra* trees. Since there is neither a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) nor a purpose (*prayojana*) regarding this matter, this entire chapter should not be studied at all.

It is said: the great purpose of this treatise (*śāstra*) is established by all of this. Herein are explained the states of transmigratory existence, from Brahmā down to the stationary beings, which have dharma and adharma as their causes;
for it will say: "Enveloped by manifold darkness, [beings are bound] by the cause of karma" (MDh 1.49).
And he will further state:
"Having observed these destinies of the living being by means of his own mind—both those resulting from righteousness and those from unrighteousness—one should always fix the mind upon righteousness.

(MDh 12.23) Therefore, since dharma is the cause of unsurpassed sovereignty and adharma is its opposite, this scripture, which possesses great purpose for the sake of thoroughly understanding their nature, must be studied; such is the purport of this chapter. As for the aphorism here, it consists of mantras, arthavādas, and general inference (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). And so, there is a mantra:

Darkness was hidden by darkness in the beginning; all this was an indistinguishable ocean. That which was covered by the void—that One, through the power of heat (*tapas*), came into being. (RV 10.129.3)

When the external and internal luminaries, such as the moon, sun, and fire, had perished at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), there was only darkness. That darkness, moreover, became shrouded by a grosser form of darkness. For at that time, there was no knower whatsoever; thus, because of the absence of a knower, there was no knowledge for anyone, and so it is said to be "shrouded by darkness. Before the creation of beings, O Agni, everything was unmanifest (*apra-keta*) and unknown. This water—meaning whatever possesses the nature of flowing, whatever is active, and whatever has motion—all that was motionless. By the "insubstantial" (*tuccha*), which means the subtle, the "substantial" (*abhū*)—the gross—was covered; the meaning is that the specific forms were dissolved within the self of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). By this much, the undifferentiated state (*avyākṛtāvasthā*) of the world is illuminated. With the fourth quarter, the initial state of creation is described: that which was "one" through the greatness (*mahan*) or majesty of austerity (*tapas*) was born; it manifested with a specific nature. The meaning is that it appeared again due to the power of *karman*. Alternatively, in that state, through the greatness of the act of austerity, Hiraṇyagarbha was born as the Self; he appeared. As it will be said: "Then the Self-existent One" (MDh 1.6).

By means of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), even a great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is rendered possible. For when destruction is observed in one part of something, the destruction of that whole is also seen; just as a house is sometimes seen burning, and at other times an entire village is consumed by fire. Furthermore, all things preceded by an agent (*kartṛpūrva*) are perishable, such as houses and palaces. This world, consisting of rivers, oceans, mountains, and so forth, is likewise preceded by an agent. Therefore, it is inferred that it will perish just like houses and the like. If it is argued that its being preceded by an agent is not established, we reply that this too is proven—just as in the case of houses—by its possessing a specific arrangement (*niveśaviśeṣa*) and other such characteristics; such is the inference based on general observation.

Nor do we exert ourselves toward the purification of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or its refutation, because this treatise has as its primary aim the absence of censure (*anindā*). For as long as this is not investigated and determined, it cannot be properly understood. And if it were so investigated, it would become a treatise on logic (*tarka-śāstra*) rather than a treatise on dharma (*dharma-śāstra*), and the work would result in excessive prolixity.

All of this will be presented with a profusion of formal procedures (*prakriyā*): in some places the ancient method (*paurāṇī prakriyā*), and in others that of the Sāṃkhyas. Whether these are understood or not understood makes no difference whatsoever to the distinction between merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); therefore, they are not analyzed with technical precision. If there is a desire for them, they should be sought from those very sources. We shall, however, provide only the explanation consisting of the coordination of the meanings of the words (*padārtha-yojanā*) as taught in this chapter; that alone we shall do. The intended purport (*tātparya*) has already been demonstrated.

This world was then as if enveloped in darkness. Although the word *bhūta* has many meanings, it is used here in the sense of a comparison; for example, in the phrase, "That which is undivided among things divided, uncut among things cut, being the universal (*sāmānyabhūta*), that is the Word," the term *sāmānyabhūta* means "like a universal. What is the similarity between the world and darkness? To this he says: "unknown" (*aprajñātam*). Because the specific natures and modifications have dissolved back into their primal source (*prakṛti*), it is therefore unknown through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Might it then be known through inference (*anumāna*)? That too is "without characteristic" (*alakṣaṇa*). A "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is a mark or sign, and even that has utterly perished in that state, because all modifications have been destroyed in their specific forms. It is "inconceivable" (*apratarkya*); its nature cannot even be conceived as such. This negates inference by way of reasoning (*tarka*). There is no inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*); nor is there any based on specific observation (*viśeṣato dṛṣṭa*) that could reveal its form; and thus it is "unknowable" (*avijñeya*).

In that case, one might conclude that [the world] did not exist at all, but was produced from non-existence; this [view] is refuted by the statement: "As if sleeping on all sides. There is no production of the existent from the non-existent. And it has been stated in the Upaniṣads, such as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. How could the existent be born from the non-existent? (ChU 6.2.1–2). Therefore, it is unknowable by means of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whose objects are limited [to empirical categories]. It is understood only from such scripture (*āgama*). The state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is like being asleep—having abandoned the states of waking and dreaming—is employed as an illustration. Just as "this self remains in the state of deep sleep with all conceptual constructions destroyed and free from the affliction of awareness, yet it cannot be said that it does not exist, because for one who has awakened there is the recognition: 'I slept happily,'" so too the world is determined through scripture—which consists of established facts—and through the fallacious inferences of logicians. "It existed" (*āsīt*): but that present state is not knowable by anyone; therefore it is called "unknowable" (*avijñeya*). "On all sides" (*sarvataḥ*) means that it is not a partial dissolution. 1.5.
Then the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, unmanifest yet making this world manifest, whose power acts upon the great elements and the rest, appeared as the dispeller of darkness.

Immediately following that great night (*mahārātri*): he is *svayaṃbhū*, meaning self-existent. He assumes a body by his own will; unlike the transmigrating soul (*saṃsāryātman*), his assumption of a body is not dependent on karma. He is *avyakta*, unmanifest—that is, invisible to those who lack the cultivation of the practice of meditative yoga (*dhyāna-yoga*). Alternatively, the text should be read as "this was unmanifest" (*avyaktam idam*). Making this unmanifest state manifest, he brings it into visibility through gross forms and transformations. By his will, the world appears once again. It "appeared" (*prādur āsīt*); the word *prāduḥ* denotes manifestation. He is the "dispeller of darkness" (*tamonuda*). "Darkness" (*tamas*) refers to the state of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); he dispels or destroys that, and creates the world anew, and is therefore called the dispeller of darkness. The "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*) are earth and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), their qualities—sound and the rest—are understood. He is described as such because his vigor (*ojas*), power (*vīrya*), and creative capacity have entered into or reached them. The great elements are themselves incapable of producing the world; however, when power is infused into them by him, they undergo transformation into the form of trees and other things. But it is not the great elements in their primordial state of potentiality, having assumed the form of *prakṛti*, that are intended here by the term "great elements" at the beginning of the world-creation. There is an alternative reading: "mahābhūtānuvṛttaujāḥ. "Anuvṛtta" means followed or entered; thus the meaning is exactly as stated before. (1.6)
He who is perceivable by those beyond the senses, subtle, unmanifest, eternal, consisting of all beings, and inconceivable—he himself has now appeared. 1.7.

By means of the two pronouns *yaḥ* and *asau*, he points toward the Supreme Brahman as if it were generally well-known. That which is well-known in the Vedāntas, in other spiritual sciences (*adhyātmavidyā*), and in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas—being characterized by the attributes about to be described—that very one is said here to have "manifested" (*prādur āsīt*). He manifested himself; he arose, that is, he took on a body. The root *bhā* has many meanings, and here it functions in the sense of arising. Alternatively, it simply means "to shine. He was self-luminous, not dependent upon the light of the sun or other sources. *Atīndriyam* is a compound meaning "beyond the senses" (*avyayībhāva*). *Atīndriyagrāhyaḥ* is a compound formed according to the rule *sup-supā* ("noun with noun"), meaning "graspable by that which transcends the senses. It is grasped by transcending the senses; it is never within the range of the [ordinary] senses. It is grasped by a completely different kind of knowledge born of yoga (*yogaja-jñāna*). Or else, "beyond the senses" refers to the mind (*manas*) which has transcended the senses. Because the senses are imperceptible, [the Self] is not their object. And just as the Vaiśeṣikas accept the inferential nature of the mind, stating: "The non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark of the mind" (*Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.16), so too is it grasped by that [mind]. Thus says the venerable Vyāsa: *...* (text follows)

"He is not grasped by the eye, nor indeed by the other sense organs; however, he is perceived by those who see the subtle with a tranquil mind. "With a tranquil mind" means one that is unstained by defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like, having acquired the power of subtle vision through being intent upon his worship. "Subtle" (*sūkṣma*) is like the atom (*anu*); for he is not the locus of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "minute," "gross," and so forth, since he transcends all conceptual constructions. And it has been said:
He who does not abide even in the appearance of any conceptual constructions,
though he has been conceptually constructed in many ways through reasoning, scripture, and inference.
"Transcending difference and connection, existence and non-existence, succession and simultaneity, as well as truth and falsehood—the Soul of the universe shines forth through discernment.

Thus, being subtle, it is unspoken; it is eternal and endowed with an unmanifest, natural sovereignty that is without beginning or end. Even for those who hold that the station of Hiraṇyagarbha is attainable through karma, in their view too there is eternality, because although it has a beginning, it lacks an end. For the state of being the enjoyer of the fruits of creation and so forth never departs.

One whose mind is thus cultivated with the thought, "I must create all beings," being the very self of all beings (*bhūtātmā*) and having become such, is said to be "composed of all beings" (*sarvabhūtamaya*). Just as a clay pot, because it is a modification of clay, has a body begun by clay and is thus called "made of clay," so too, whoever intensely contemplates anything becomes "composed of that" through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). For example: "this man is composed of women," or "composed of the *Ṛgveda*," or "composed of the *Yajurveda*. Alternatively, according to the non-dualistic (*advaita*) view: sentient and insentient beings do not exist as separate entities; rather, this [universe] is the illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of That alone. Therefore, since illusory manifestations are composed of those [beings] and are non-different from them, their being "composed of those" is entirely logical. But how can the manifestation of manifold forms from a single [reality], which seems contradictory due to its unity, be explained? Those who maintain the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavādins*) say this: just as waves arise from the ocean when struck by the wind, and they are neither different from it nor yet untouched by it—they are in every way indefinable in terms of identity or difference—so too is this the universal illusory manifestation of Brahman. The word "also" (*api*) should be understood here: while remaining in its own nature it is ungraspable, yet in the state of illusory manifestation it is graspable by the senses. Thus it is subtle; and by virtue of the word "also," it is gross in its gross state. It is unmanifest and manifest, eternal and non-eternal, composed of beings and yet devoid of their form. This is to be explained solely through the distinctions of the states of illusory manifestation.
It is inconceivable and of a wondrous nature, due to its union with a power that is distinct from all [other] characteristics. 1.7.
Desiring to create various kinds of beings, he, having meditated, first emitted water from his own body; into that water, he cast his seed. (1.8)

He, having obtained the name *Hiraṇyagarbha* through the mantras previously specified, such as "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose" (*RV* 10.121.1), desiring to create—that is, wishing to bring forth—various creatures of manifold forms, first created the waters, that is, water. [The question arises: from his own body, which body did he take? In the Advaita philosophy, *pradhāna* itself is his body, because it conforms to his will and is the cause of the creation of his body by its very nature. Did he create the bodies of all worlds through material activity, such as digging with a spade? No, he says; how then? By mere thought (*abhidhyāya*). That is, by the mere wish: "Let the waters come into being. Here it is further asked: since earth and the other elements did not yet exist at that time, what was the support for the waters that were created? To this it is replied: one must also state what the support was for the Creator, the Supreme Lord, who had assumed a body. Or rather, due to the possession of a distinct and superior sovereignty, that power of agency is entirely different and beyond questioning, unlike the common properties of ordinary matter; thus it should be understood even in these cases. Into those waters, he cast—that is, poured—his seed (*vīrya*). 1.8.
That egg became golden, possessing a radiance equal to the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.

First, the primary matter (*pradhāna*), which exists everywhere, becomes earth in form. Through conjunction with the seed-potency (*vīrya*) of Hiraṇyagarbha, it attains solidity; that is said to have become the egg. "Haimam" means made of gold (*svarṇamaya*). [The text says] "of that golden one" because of the commonality of its rays (*aṃśu*). [Objection]: This meaning is not based on scripture (*āgamika*), nor is the word "like" (*iva*) heard here; how then can there be an interpretation by metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) in the absence of another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? [Reply]: It will be stated: "From those two shell-parts, he fashioned heaven and earth" (MDh 1.13). Since this earth consists of clay and is not entirely made of gold, metaphorical usage is resorted to. "Sahasrāṃśuḥ" means the Sun; the egg's radiance or luster is equal to his rays. In that egg, Brahmā himself was born—meaning he came into being. Brahmā is indeed Hiraṇyagarbha himself. The word "himself" (*svayam*) has already been explained. By the power of yoga, having cast off the body previously assumed, he entered within the egg. Or else, being bodiless, he first created the waters; then, within the egg, he took up his own body.

Alternatively, he who is indicated by the words "he who" (MDh 1.7) is one, while this "egg-born Brahmā" is another; for the author will later state, "emitted by him" (MDh 1.11), meaning created by that Lord (Īśvara). If so, how is it that Brahmā is described there as having been "born of himself" and being "self-existent"? This is not a fault. A son is designated by the name of his father, as in the Vedic passage: "The Self was born from the Self. The Teacher has recorded these [statements] from scriptures whose primary intent is not to describe the ultimate reality (*anidampara*); one should not be dogmatic about them. It has already been stated that whether "he himself is born" or "another is created by him" is of no consequence for the exposition of Dharma. He is known by the name "Grandfather of all worlds" (*sarvalokapitāmaha*). Because he is regarded as a father through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), even though it is not literal, he is the "Grandfather" (*pitāmaha*) and is thus more venerable than even a biological father. (1.9)
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
since they were his first place of resort (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. (1.10)

He who is proclaimed in the Agamas by the word *Nārāyaṇa*—due to his possession of an excellence of power as both agent and knower—as the Puruṣa who is the cause of the universe, is this very one. There is no difference in meaning due to a difference in words. Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Maheśvara are one and the same reality; they do not differ merely as objects of worship. We shall demonstrate this in the twelfth [chapter]. And thus it is said accordingly: "The waters were called *nārāḥ*. Now, one might object: "This is not the usage of the elders, nor is it well-known in that sense. To this he says: "The waters are indeed the offspring (*sūnavaḥ*) of *nara*. That Blessed One is well-known as *nara*, the Puruṣa. And the waters are his offspring, his progeny; therefore, they are designated by the word *nara*. For the word for "father" is seen to be applied to the offspring: the offspring of Vasiṣṭha are "Vasiṣṭhas," the offspring of Bhṛgu are "Bhṛgus," and likewise, through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), those waters are denoted by the word *nara*, as in the case of "Babhrumaṇḍulomaka. Because he was formerly the *ayana*—the path, the first creation, or the support—of this Prajāpati while he was in the womb, for that reason he is remembered as *Nārāyaṇa*. When the form *narāyaṇaḥ* would have resulted from the analysis "his *ayana* is *nara*," the lengthening of the vowel occurs according to Pāṇini 6.3.137: "it is also seen in other cases," just as in the word *puruṣaḥ*. Alternatively, the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of a collection (*sāmūhika*). 1.10.
That cause which is unmanifest, eternal, and consisting of both the existent and the non-existent—
the Puruṣa created from that is celebrated in the world as Brahman.

It is the cause alone, not the effect, nor is its body subject to the will of another; it is endowed with its own natural majesty. It is said to be unmanifest and eternal—the meaning of which has already been explained. It consists of both being and non-being (*sadasadātmaka*). "Being" (*sat*) and "non-being" (*asat*) constitute the pair *sadasat*; that whose nature (*ātmā*) or essence is these two is so described. But how can there be the conjunction of two contradictory properties—existence and non-existence—in a single entity? It is replied: for those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*), because there is no perception of it as an object, it is unfit for the conventional usage of existence and is thus called "of the nature of non-being. From the scriptures (*āgama*), however, because it is understood to be the cause of all this, it is of the nature of being. Therefore, due to the difference in the cognizer, the dual usage regarding Brahman is not contradictory in either respect.

But surely, all things whatsoever are of such a nature that they are always existent by their own form and non-existent by the form of another. Why, then, is it said that this is "not contradictory in the case of Brahman"? It is replied: in the vision of non-duality (*advaita*), there is nothing whatsoever other than Brahman; what, then, could be "other" such that its non-existence could be predicated by way of that [other] form?

The person who was emitted, produced, and fashioned within the egg by him is celebrated in the world as Brahmā. He is the one who, as is heard in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, sits here and there for the purpose of granting boons to the gods, asuras, and great sages of fierce asceticism; he is this very one who was first emitted by that Great Person, the Supreme Brahman.

Others, however, explain the passage beginning with “you alone” (*tvam evaikaḥ*, MDh 1.3) differently. By the demonstrative pronoun *asya* (of this), the world is indicated through a gesture of direct perception. The *vidhāna*—the creation or arrangement—of this entire world belongs to the Self-Existent (*svayaṃbhuva*); it is inconceivable, of wondrous form, manifold, exceedingly great, and immeasurable, such that it cannot be known by everyone. Thus says the Seer: “Who indeed knows, who here can declare, whence it was born, whence this diverse creation? (RV 10.129.6). Is this entire world produced in dependence upon a material cause (*upādāna*), or is it merely a magical emanation (*nairmāṇika*), as in the view of the Buddha? Is it dependent on the will of God, or born solely from the power of karma, or is it natural and immeasurable? Likewise, is it produced in the sequence of Mahat and the rest, or in the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth? You know its *kārya* (effect), its *tattva* (essence), and its *artha* (purpose). *Kārya*: From Mahat comes the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); from the ego-sense come the non-specific *tanmātras*; from the *tanmātras* come the specific five gross elements; and from the ego-sense come the eleven organs. The collective effect of even these specifics consists of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. The *tattva* (essence) or nature of these is their fundamental reality, just as the essence of Mahat is its state of pure form. That which is the state of modification of the whole of Pradhāna is called Mahat. *Prakṛti* and *pradhāna* have the same meaning; thus, Mahat is derived from *prakṛti*. The *tattva* of the ego-sense is its state of being mere self-consciousness (*asmipratyaya*). The *tattva* of the non-specifics is their being perceivable only as non-specific cognitions. *Artha* means purpose. This entity serves the Person (*puruṣa*) in this manner for the sake of the Person, and it accomplishes this purpose. Although knowledge of the world’s creation belonging to the Teacher is of no assistance whatsoever to one desiring to know Dharma, nor is it something that ought to be asked about, nevertheless, because the creation of the world is difficult to understand from other sources due to the diversity among the Great Sages, it is worthy of inquiry at the outset. For the mind is inexpressible. Even that object which is not within the scope of the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), you know it by means of the vision of a Seer (*ārṣa-cakṣus*). Furthermore, since Dharma is the domain of the Veda, it has certainly been understood by you. In this way, the praise of the speaker is directed precisely toward the subject matter at hand.

Thus encouraged by the hymn of praise, [the author] first speaks of the creation of the world, beginning with the words "This was" (MDh 1.5) and "Then the Self-existent" (MDh 1.6). By these terms, *pradhāna* (primordial matter) alone is denoted. It exists by itself, undergoes transformation, and enters into modification as the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *mahat*. There is no Lord established by his own nature who directs the insentient *pradhāna* according to his will; rather, this is simply the inherent nature of things—that *pradhāna*, which is of the form of *prakṛti*, undergoes further modification. Just as insentient milk becomes curd through stages such as whey (*maṇḍaka*), so it is here. Regarding the word "Bhagavān": the Lord, through his own activity, proceeds by means of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth. "Ojas" is the vigor or capacity for one's own task. The word "ādi" (etcetera) is used in the sense of variety or arrangement. By that, the unmanifest (*avyakta*) becomes the cause of *mahat* and the rest. Having fallen away from its prior state during the stage of modification, it is said to "dispel darkness" as it consists of light. Alternatively, the masculine gender is used for *pradhāna* by supplying the word "artha" (object/purpose). Furthermore, the word "puruṣa" is seen used for *pradhāna* and other such entities, as in: "Of those seven persons... (MDh 1.19).

"He who," as before; "he meditated" (*abhidhyāya*). Meditation (*abhidhyāna*) occurs by way of its qualities, because the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), being insentient, cannot itself meditate. Just as one might say that someone brings about an effect simply by meditating, so too an object transforming according to its own nature is said to "meditate" when it does not depend on the will of a Lord nor on any other causal agent. He created water first. Its status as "first" is relative to the other great elements (*mahābhūta*), but not in relation to the production of the principles beginning with *mahat*. For he will state later: "Of these seven... (MDh 1.19). First there is the production of the principles (*tattva*), and then of the elements. "In them [he placed] his seed. He emitted his seed, which is power (*śakti*). The *pradhāna* alone is the agent. Through its pervasive power, the *pradhāna* attains solidity in the production of the elements such as earth, and becomes the form of an egg. "That egg"—just as the principles were produced without the union of male and female, so too, by the force of prior karma, Brahmā’s body was produced without a womb (*ayonija*) through his own majesty alone, like a gadfly or a mosquito. "Emanated by him": it is called "emanated by him" because it was emitted by that *pradhāna*, since the body consists of that [matter]. The rest is as before.

Whatever the true meaning here may be, that has already been stated by us; these are merely explanatory passages (arthavāda) which are interpreted in some way through figurative description (guṇavāda). 1.11.
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One,
by his own meditative power, split that egg into two parts.

That Blessed Brahmā, having dwelt within that egg for a full year—that is, a *parivatsara*—and having become omniscient while remaining there, reflected: "How might I emerge? He then split that egg in two. By that much time, the embryo had matured; by that same amount of time, the egg had also reached the state of being broken due to its ripening. Therefore, it is said that he split the egg in two according to the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit (*kākatālīya-nyāya*). (1.12)
From those two fragments, he fashioned heaven and earth;
in between, the intermediate space, the eight directions, and the eternal abode of the waters.

The two halves are the two shell-parts of the egg (*aṇḍakapāla*). From those two shell-parts, he fashioned (*nirmame*) the heaven above; from the lower one, the earth; and in between, the void or sky (*vyoma*). There are also the eight directions, beginning with the east, together with the intermediate directions such as southeast and so forth. The abode of the waters is the ocean in the intermediate space, while the earth and the netherworld (*pātāla*) are situated below. (1.13)
And he drew forth from himself the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
and from the mind, the ego-sense, the lord who is the conceiver.

The creation of the principles (*tattva*) is now described. That which was previously mentioned according to its constituent parts will here be stated in reverse order; thus it has been said [in verse 45]: "From Pradhāna, he extracted the mind from his own form. This production of the principles is here stated in reverse order. Prior to the mind is the *ahaṃkāra*, the conceiving agent. The function of *ahaṃkāra* is the conceit "I am" (*aham iti abhimānitā*). It is the Lord (*īśvara*), capable of accomplishing the task. (1.14)
And [he perceives] the self as truly great, as well as all the five sense organs, which consist of the three qualities and are the perceivers of objects, [all of them] gradually. 1.15.

The principle known as *mahat* is well-established among the Sāṃkhyas by that name. The term "the Self" (*ātmānam*) is used here in grammatical apposition with "the Great One" (*mahat*). Furthermore, because it is woven through (*anusyūta*) all created bodies by virtue of its greatness, it is designated as the "Self. Prior to the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), he created [the principles] according to the previously stated method; and all things are composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*). Everything that has been enumerated or will be enumerated is characterized by the three qualities. *Sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the qualities. The knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*s), however, are exclusively devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). The entire portion consisting of primordial nature (*prākṛta*) is made up of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. The five sense organs are the perceivers of their respective objects—such as form, taste, and so forth—which are the domains of their specific designations, and they generate cognition. The five [organs] will be mentioned by their specific names starting with "the ear, the skin," etc. (MDh 2.90). By the word "and" (*ca*), the objects—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—as well as earth and the other elements, are also included. (1.15)
But having combined the subtle constituent parts of those six beings of immeasurable power with portions of his own self, he created all living beings.

Having arranged subtle constituent parts within the *ātmamātrās* (self-measures) of those six, he fashioned all beings (*sarvabhūtāni*). Here, by the number six, the five *tanmātras* to be mentioned later and the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense) that has already been discussed are indicated. Their *ātmamātrās* are their own modifications: from the *tanmātras* come the elements (*bhūtas*), and from the *ahaṃkāra* come the sense organs (*indriyas*). Having arranged the subtle constituent parts—the *tanmātras* and the *ahaṃkāra*—within the elements such as earth and so forth, which exist in the form of bodies, and having performed their placement in their respective locations, he fashioned all beings, including gods, humans, animals, birds, and stationary things. This is what is meant: the six non-specific (*aviśeṣa*) constituents are the initiators of one part [of the whole], because the entire world is originated from them. Their subtlety is established by the very designation "*tanmātra*" (mere-measure). Having arranged—that is, brought together—those [parts], he fashioned from their very *ātmamātrās*, which are their modifications, the elements and the sense organs; and by the word "and" (*ca*), the creation of the physical aggregates (*piṇḍasṛṣṭi*) is also included. Regarding the reading "in the *mātrās*" (*mātrāsu*), the reading "by the *mātrās*" (*mātrābhiḥ*) is more appropriate. (1.16)
Those six subtle components of form resort to these [elements];
therefore, the wise call that form "the body" (śarīra). 1.17

*Mūrtiḥ* means the body (*śarīra*). Its *arthāḥ* are the constituent parts that bring it about. The subtle ones are the six whose natures have been described and which are called the *aviśeṣas*. These [subtle elements] and the sense organs (*indriya*) to be mentioned hereafter depend upon the gross elements (*bhūta*). It is said that they "depend upon the elements because of their arising from them. Their arising has those [elements] as its support. And it is recited: "From the five [subtle elements], the five gross elements [arise]" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 22). Because they depend on them for that reason, the body—which is the form (*mūrti*) of that primary cause (*pradhāna*)—is called the "body. *Manīṣiṇaḥ*: *Manīṣā* is the intellect (*buddhi*); those who possess it are the wise. Alternatively, the agency is reversed: the subtle [elements] are the agents and the sense organs are the object. And the constituent parts, by attaining the state of being the support for the sense organs, are said to "depend. Just as one says, "he was eaten by many," meaning he ate while causing others to eat. Or, since verbal roots have multiple meanings, "they depend" means "they produce. (1.17)
Then the great elements, together with their functions, enter that imperishable creator of all beings, along with the mind and its subtle constituents. 1.18.

This very *pradhāna* becomes the creator of all beings; it is imperishable (*avyaya*) and indestructible (*avināśa*) in its causal form. How does it create all beings? Because these [beings] enter into it. What, then, are they? The mind (*manas*), together with its subtle components—the *tanmātras* characterized as intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the senses; immediately following these, the great elements known as earth, water, fire, air, and ether; and along with their functions (*karmāṇi*). The functions of earth and the others are, respectively: support (*dhṛti*), cohesion (*saṃhanana*), digestion (*pakti*), arrangement (*vyūha*), and space (*avakāśa*). Among these, *dhṛti* is supporting—that is, the maintenance in one place of that which would otherwise have the nature of flowing away or falling down. *Saṃhanana* is the gathering together of what was scattered by means of a binder, just as scattered dust particles are gathered and formed into a mass by water. *Pakti* (digestion) is well known as the effect of fire upon food, medicinal herbs, grass, and so forth. *Vyūha* is arrangement or configuration. *Avakāśa* is non-obstruction by another corporeal object; for in whatever place one corporeal object is situated, there is no room for another corporeal object. Indeed, within a lump of gold, nothing else can exist inside. The mention of the "mind" (*manas*) is for the purpose of indicating all the sense organs (*indriya*). Furthermore, by the mention of "functions," the organs of action (*karmendriya*) are understood. Alternatively, the construction may be understood thus: subsequently, it presides over the great elements which are joined with their subtle components and their effects. And the sense organs are included because the word "mind" is intended to indicate them all. (1.18)
But from these seven immensely powerful beings,
the perishable arises from the imperishable through the subtle constituent elements of form.

The meaning is simply this: the gross arises from the subtle; the perishable [proceeds] from the imperishable. It does not mean "from the measures (mātrās) of six or seven principles. There are twenty-four principles (*tattvas*). These are the cause of everything in creation. Alternatively, in the creation of the body (*piṇḍasṛṣṭi*), only seven are the primary causes: the six non-specific (*aviśeṣa*) principles and the seventh, the Great One (*mahat*). From these, the elements and the sense organs arise. Once they have arisen, the body becomes a solid mass.

From the imperishable *pradhāna*, which has accumulated all modifications (*vikāra*) and is unified, this world—possessing manifold forms and scattered in many ways—is produced. Does the *pradhāna* undergo transformation simultaneously with all its gross-form modifications? No, he says: "Of these, this [is so]," meaning by that very sequence previously described: "From *prakṛti* comes the Great One (*mahat*); from that, the I-maker (*ahaṃkāra*); from that, the group of sixteen" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 22). The word *puruṣa* is applied to the principle (*tattva*) because it exists for the sake of the *puruṣa* (the Spirit). [The term *mahaujasaḥ* refers to those] powerful in their own effects. It is called "Great" (*mahat*) because it is the cause of immeasurable modifications. From their subtle portions of form—that is, their bodies—the [gross] form arises; it is for the sake of those [subtle] portions that this [world] comes into being. Therefore it is said: "From the imperishable, the perishable. But what are their subtle portions? For there can be no other portions of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) such that a distinction like "their subtle portions" would be logical. Nor do they depend on their own portions. What then? [It means: the Great One (*mahat*) is subtler than the subtle elements, and the Source (*prabhu*) is subtler than the Great One. 1.19.
Each subsequent one among these acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever of them occupies which position in the sequence, it is traditionally held to possess that many qualities. (1.20)

In the preceding verse, some interpret the number seven differently: the five sense organs, beginning with the eye, when grouped together, become one; they are designated as a single unit because of their connection with the single factor that is the cause of cognition. The same applies to the organs of action. Since these two groups are distinct, they constitute two persons. The five elements are specified separately due to the diversity of their functions. Thus, there are seven persons. Their "forms" (*mūrti*) consist of the subtle essences (*tanmātra*), which are the effects of manifestation, along with the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*). The rest is the same.

And therefore, because the elements (*bhūta*) were mentioned in the preceding verse, the word "of these" (*eṣām*) refers back to them. Although many intervening statements are present, nevertheless, the point established here—that the possession of specific number, agent, and quality—is possible only for the elements and not for others, even though they were also under discussion.

Therefore, this is the meaning of the verse: among these elements (*bhūta*), whatever is the first of each [subsequent element], the form that is recited immediately after it takes on the quality (*guṇa*) of the preceding one through connection. By the word "quality," the five—sound and the rest—are meant. And here, "being first" is according to the order to be stated later: "ether is born" (MDh 1.75). He will also state right there that sound and the others are qualities. Whatever object characterized by ether and so forth occupies a certain ordinal position—that is, completes a certain number—"vator ithuk" (Pāṇ 5.2.53)—if it stands in the second or third position, it possesses that many qualities; it has as many qualities as its place. For example, standing in the second position, it is two-fold, and so on. The fact that they are mutually connected with the first quality of each was stated in the first half-verse. In that context, whichever quality is expressed for a specific element by its own name—as in "they know its quality to be sound" (MDh 1.75) or "that is said to have the quality of form" (MDh 1.77)—then, upon acquiring the preceding quality, a doubling occurs for the elements, with the exception of ether. Therefore it is said: "whatever occupies a certain ordinal position. By this, air is two-fold, fire is three-fold, water is four-fold, and earth is five-fold. How is the expression *ādyādyasya* ("of each first") to be understood? It should be *ādyasyādyasya* ("of each first"), using the double mention (*dvirvacana*) according to the rule "for the constant and the distributive" (*nityavīpsayoḥ*). Just as in the case of *paraḥ paraḥ*. Because there is no distinction in the Smṛtis from Vedic meters (*chandas*), and for the sake of following the established usage (*vṛtta*), it is thus recited. (1.20)
But at the beginning, he fashioned the names and the distinct actions of all beings, as well as their separate conditions, from the words of the Veda itself.

That Prajāpati gave names to all things, just as someone gives names to sons who have been born or to other things for the sake of worldly transaction, such as: *vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1) or *dhī-śrī-strī-m* (Piṅgala 1.1.1). He established the relationship between words and their meanings, such as "cow," "horse," and "man. He also fashioned ritual acts (*karman*), namely those called merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) which have unseen results (*adṛṣṭārtha*), such as the Agnihotra and others. Having created these rituals, he established their specific arrangements and regulations therein: "This ritual must be performed by a Brāhmaṇa alone at this particular time for the sake of this specific fruit. Alternatively, there are regulations (*saṃsthā*) with visible purposes (*dṛṣṭārtha*), such as: "Cattle-grazing must not be carried out in this region," or "This water must not be given for irrigation in that village until we have received this favor from that village. He also fashioned rituals with visible purposes. Among those, the ones with unseen purposes [are known] from Vedic words or Vedic sentences.

But surely, since everything was created by Him alone and He possesses absolute sovereignty, one must say that He created this Veda for the purpose of maintaining the performance of ritual acts; and the creation of the Veda will indeed be described in the intervening passage beginning with "and from fire, wind, and the sun" (MDh 1.23).

It is said: there are differing views on this matter. Some say that in another *kalpa* the Vedas were studied by him, and they were dissolved during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Then, in another *kalpa*, everything appears anew, like one waking from sleep; just as a verse previously recited in a dream might appear to someone. Furthermore, it appears in the Veda through such sentences as "A bull is to be bound for sacrifice" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 10.4.32) and "The horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal" (*Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā* 24.1). Having suddenly remembered those meanings preceded by the recollection of the words, and having seen the objects being produced, he created both names and ritual actions from the very words of the Veda, thinking: "This word was the name for this object in another *kalpa*; let it be used for this very thing now. Alternatively, the Vedas do not dissolve even at the great dissolution. That Puruṣa who is accepted by some [as the creator] exists in the same manner as the Vedas. He himself, having fashioned the Puruṣa within the egg who is identical with Brahman, taught him the Vedas. Thus, that Brahmā created everything from the words of the Veda.

Whatever the truth in this matter is, that has already been stated by us. Now, if the Puranic method is employed, that too is indeed being demonstrated by us: first, the creation of the world—this is the meaning. Or else, "first" refers to those names which are uncorrupted, and not the modern ones such as *gavi* and so forth, which arise from incapacity. "Separately" (*pṛthak*): he did not fashion [them] in the same way as the body, which is a mere collection of principles (*tattva*); rather, [he fashioned them] separately. (1.21)
The Lord created the gods whose nature is action, as well as living beings;
he also created the subtle host of Sādhyas and the eternal sacrifice.

Those embodied beings who are devoted to ritual actions (*karman*) are called "action-natures" (*karmātmānaḥ*), namely human beings intent upon such deeds. For the sake of accomplishing their goals, he created sacrifice (*yajña*). Those who take no delight in the meditations on Brahman (*brahmopāsanā*), who seek fruits such as sons and cattle, and who rely on the dualistic position—they are called "action-natures" because they are devoted to the performance of rituals. Since the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) can express the sense of "for the purpose of that" (*tādarthya*), it is understood that "he created sacrifice for their sake. He also created the host of gods (*devagaṇa*) for that same purpose. The word "and" (*ca*) is placed out of its proper order after "of the action-natures"; its proper place is immediately after "of the gods. He created the sacrifice; he created the host of gods—beginning with Agni, Agni-Soma, Indra-Agni, and so forth—for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice. Likewise, the phrase "the host of the Sādhyas" is to be supplied. They are mentioned separately because they do not partake of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*); they are merely recipients of praise, as in: "Where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide" (RV 10.90.16), "The gods named Sādhyas," and "There were indeed gods named Sādhyas" (PB 8.3.5). Alternatively, it is like the expression "Brahmins and wandering mendicants" (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka*): compared to the Maruts, Rudras, and Aṅgirasas, the host of Sādhyas is subtle. The mention of the Sādhyas is intended to indicate other deities as well who are not connected with the sacrificial oblation, such as those addressed in the verses beginning with *venas tuṣṭim*.

Others, however, consider these terms to be in apposition with "gods" and "living beings," [interpreting them as] "those whose self is karma. Those for whom karma is the self—that is, the acquisition of their own nature—are "karmātmanas. Alternatively, they are "karmātmanas" because they are primarily intent upon the performance of rituals such as sacrifices.
