Certain deities are mentioned in the *itihāsas* by their very nature (*svarūpataḥ*) in connection with rituals such as sacrifices, such as Indra, Rudra, and Viṣṇu. For others, however, deityhood exists only in the context of the sacrifice and not by their own nature, as in the case of the dice, the pressing-stones, and the parts of a chariot; for the deeds of Indra and others—such as their battles with the Asuras like Vṛtra—are recounted in the *Mahābhārata*, whereas such deeds are not described for the dice and the rest. Nevertheless, they possess deityhood in relation to the oblation within a *sūkta*, as in the case of the dice: "O trembling ones, [protect] me" (*prāvepā mā*, RV 10.34.1); of the pressing-stones: "Let these speak forth" (*praite vadantu*, RV 10.94.1); and of the chariot-parts: "O tree, firm-limbed one" (*vanaspate vīḍvaṅgaḥ*, RV 6.47.26). Therefore, [the text says] "of living beings. Deities are indeed of two kinds: those possessing breath (*prāṇavatī*) and those devoid of it. Just as Indra and others are described in the Purāṇas as having human forms and possessing breath, the dice and others are not. Furthermore, this entire expansion of creation and so forth is based on the perspective of the *itihāsas*. The word "and" (*ca*) should be understood here [to include] both living and non-living beings. In the *Nirukta* tradition as well, deities are of two kinds: the horse in "May no enemy... (*mā no amitraḥ*, RV 1.162.1); the bird in "Crying out... (*kanikradat*, RV 5.83.1); and the cows in "The cows have come" (*ā gāvo agman*, RV 6.28.2). These are the ones possessing breath. Those without breath have been mentioned [above]. The inclusion of the word "eternal" (*sanātana*) is an epithet of the sacrifice; for since the sacrifice existed even in previous *kalpas*, its eternity is due to its continuous flow (*pravāha*). 1.22.
From fire, wind, and the sun, he milked forth the threefold eternal Brahman,
characterized as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, for the sake of accomplishing sacrifice.

"There are only three deities," beginning with Agni, according to the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*), even though there is a plurality of names. Therefore, it is stated according to that view: for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice from these three [deities]. Because they are the recipients of the sacrifice (*yāga-saṃpradāna*), the dative case is used for them. He milked the triple Brahman known as the Veda, characterized by the *Ṛc*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman*. This verbal root takes two objects. The primary object is the triad; there ought to be a secondary object, but such one does not exist. Therefore, we consider this to be the ablative case alone: he milked, i.e., he caused to flow forth or brought into being, from Agni and the others.
But how could sounds consisting of phonemes, such as fire (*agni*) and so forth, become mantra-sentences and Brāhmaṇa-sentences?
What is not possible here? Who is capable of asserting unobserved and non-existent potencies (*śakti*)?

It is not proper to conceptualize the meaning of a verbal root (*ākhyāta*). In that case, what is the purpose of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) [in Pāṇini’s rule]? According to the rule *duhi-yāci-*, there ought to be an accusative case. Furthermore, a past event being described in a way that contradicts observed means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not bring satisfaction to the minds of those who rely on authority (*prāmāṇika*).

The contradiction has been resolved by resorting to the view that these scriptural passages are intent upon [describing] the essential nature [of the Vedas], as in: "The Ṛgveda was born from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vāyu, and the Sāmaveda from Āditya" (AitB 25.7). Since even deities such as Agni possess lordly power and Prajāpati possesses unsurpassed power, what inconsistency could there possibly be? In this view, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is also intended to be expressed. Thus, those [grammatical] factors which have been designated as *kārakas* where the technical term *apādāna* applies were justified in the Bhāṣya (on Pāṇini 1.4.51) when the intention to express the *apādāna* is present. How, then, is it explained in the other view?

The fourth [interpretation] is indeed appropriate; moreover, these are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). In that regard, the second action is the self itself, as in: "Prajāpati milked himself. And "milking" here refers to teaching, by virtue of the commonality of transferring [knowledge] to another.

Furthermore, there is also the fifth [reason]. In that regard, the *mantras* dedicated to Agni appear at the beginning of the *Ṛgveda*, and thus it is said, "From Agni he was born" (*AitB* 5.32). Likewise, in the *Yajurveda*, it says, "For food thee, for strength thee" (*TS* 1.1.1). *Iḍ* is food; because it resides in the middle [region], it is produced by Vāyu through the giving of rain. *Ūrj* is vital breath (*prāṇa*), and that is indeed Vāyu. Therefore, because of the connection with the activity of Vāyu from the very beginning, there is the comparison "from Vāyu. Alternatively, since the office of the *adhvaryu* priest, the sacrificial duties, and all the various types of ritual movements belong to Vāyu, the birth of the *Yajurveda* is from Vāyu by virtue of this commonality. Because one who lacks authority is unfit for the singing of the *Sāmans*, the *Sāmans* are the highest forms of study, and the Sun occupies the highest station. || 23 ||
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the rivers, the oceans, and the mountains; and the level and uneven terrains.

He speaks because of the commonality of their nature as phenomena (*dharma*). Time is, for the Vaiśeṣikas, a substantial entity (*dravyātman*); for others, it is of the nature of action (*kriyārūpa*). It consists of the extension of the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies, and it possesses recurrence. The divisions of time are its distinctions, such as months, seasons, solstices (*ayana*), years, and so forth. The lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) are Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and the rest. The planets (*graha*) are the sun and the others. The rivers (*sarit*) are the streams. The oceans (*sāgara*) are the seas. The mountains (*śaila*) are the peaks. The plains (*sama*) are level ground, uniform regions of earth free from excavations and chasms. The uneven (*viṣama*) are those possessing ascents and descents. (1.24)
Desiring to create these progeny, he emitted this creation: austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger. || 1.25 ||

*Rati* is the satisfaction of the mind; *kāma* is longing or desire, or else the god of love (*manmatha*). The rest is well known. He created this creation beginning with these. In this verse, both the creation previously mentioned and this one are intended. The meaning is that, desiring to create these offspring—namely the gods, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and so forth—he first created their instruments, as well as their bodies and their *dharma*, which possess the very nature of those [beings]. Now, what is the grammatical construction of the phrase "he created the creation" (*sṛṣṭiṃ sasṛje*)? It is the same meaning as "he performed creation" (*sṛṣṭiṃ cakāra*). All verbal roots (*dhātavaḥ*) function to denote a specific instance of the general sense of "doing. For example, *pacati* means "he performs cooking," and *yajati* means "he performs sacrifice. In such cases, once the specific action is understood from the nominal derivative (*kṛdanta*), the verbal root within the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) serves merely to convey the general sense of "doing. Even when that general sense is already understood from some other source, there is no fault of tautology (*anuvāda*) in restating it; rather, the purpose lies in specifying the time, the agent, and other such factors. Alternatively, the "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) qualified by the specific objects being created and delimited by the means of knowledge is the object of the general act of creating, just as in the expression "he nourished his own prosperity" (*svapoṣaṃ puṣṭaḥ*). || 25 ||
For the sake of distinguishing between karmas, he separated dharma and adharma;
and he joined these creatures with pairs such as pleasure and pain.

He distinguished between *dharma* and *adharma*, establishing them through differentiation as distinct entities: "This is indeed *dharma*; this is indeed *adharma*. But is it not the case that such a distinction does not exist? For there are actions of a dual nature, consisting of both *dharma* and *adharma*. As they say: "Vedic rituals are variegated (*śabala*), because they have violence as their means; for example, the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is *dharma* in its essential form, yet it is *adharma* because violence is an auxiliary part of it."

Therefore, he says: "But for the sake of distinguishing actions (*karma*). Here, by the word *karman*, the performance or application of actions is meant. That very same thing, when applied differently, becomes of a contrary nature: that which is *dharma* assumes the form of *adharma*, and *adharma* attains the state of *dharma*. For instance, violence (*hiṃsā*) itself: violence performed externally is *adharma*, because it falls within the scope of the prohibition, "One must not harm any living beings. However, [violence] performed within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*) during the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice is *dharma*, because it is characterized by a scriptural injunction (*vidhi*). Likewise, austerity (*tapas*) is *dharma*; yet that very same austerity, when performed out of hypocrisy or due to incapacity and so forth, is *adharma*. Similarly, for women, approaching a deity is *adharma*; but for those commissioned by their elders and desiring offspring, it is *dharma* through the favor of being anointed with clarified butter and so on. Therefore, even though the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is one, the distinction between *dharma* and *adharma* is established through the difference in application (*prayoga*). Even where there is unity, the difference in essential nature is seen from the perspective of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Moreover, the word "action" (*karman*) is used here for the fruits of action, by way of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the effect. By this, it is meant that he distinguished actions for the sake of differentiating their fruits. What, then, is this differentiation of the fruits of actions? To this it is said: "He joined them with pairs, such as pleasure and pain. Pleasure is the fruit of *dharma*, and pain is the fruit of *adharma*. Therefore, those who perform both are joined with pairs: because of performing *dharma* they are joined with pleasure, and because of performing *adharma* they are joined with pain. This term "pair" (*dvandva*) is used by convention to denote mutually opposed things that cause affliction, such as cold and heat, rain and sun, hunger and satiety, and so forth. The inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) should be understood as referring to the relationship between general categories and specific instances. Alternatively, the words "pleasure" and "pain" alone may signify heaven and hell, denoting unsurpassed bliss and torment. The specific scope of the word "etcetera" includes the acquisition of heaven, villages, sons, cattle, and the like, as well as their loss. The prior arising of actions has already been described; by this verse, the distinction is established that Prajāpati performed the classification of their application and the differentiation of their fruits. (1.26)
The minute, perishable particles which are said to belong to the five [elements]—with these together, all this comes into being in successive order. (1.27)

This is the summary: the subtle (aṇvyaḥ), minute (sūkṣmāḥ) measures (mātrāḥ)—that is, the constituent parts (avayavāḥ) called *tanmātras*—of the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūtāni*), which number ten when halved, are perishable. Because they possess the nature of transformation (*pariṇāma-dharmitvāt*), they are said to be imperishable through their attainment of grossness. Together with these, this entire world comes into being and arises "in succession" (*anupūrvaśaḥ*), that is, by degrees—from the subtle to the gross, and from the gross to the grosser; or rather, in the same order as was previously stated. (1.27)
Whatever task the Lord first appointed him to perform,
that very same task he himself undertook again and again as he was being created.

This is its meaning: although Prajāpati, as the Lord, is capable of creating living beings at will during the creation of the elements, he nevertheless does not create living beings without regard for the *karma* performed in previous *kalpas*. He causes a person to be born into that specific birth-class (*jāti*) projected by whatever kind of *karma* was performed by them in a prior *kalpa*, and not into another birth-class. By means of auspicious *karma*, he causes them to be born into birth-classes such as gods or humans, which are fit for the enjoyment of its fruit; by the opposite [unwholesome] *karma*, [he causes them to be born] among animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth. Just as the elements, sense-faculties, and qualities, existing in their primordial nature (*prakṛti*), emerge at the beginning of a *kalpa*, so too do *karmas* exist in their own primordial nature during the dissolution and emerge again at the beginning of creation. The principle expressed in the rule "then by the remainder" applies there as well.

If, then, origination depends upon karma, where is the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of Prajāpati useful, or what kind of dependent sovereignty is it? Since the world originates when he exists, how can his sovereignty be useless? Without him, there are no persistence, origination, or dissolution. Because he is eternal, even the karmas performed by beings themselves are causes, as are his will and the transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). From this collection of causes, this world arises, persists, and dissolves. Even though his sovereignty is dependent [on other factors], it is not impaired. Just as a king or similar sovereign here on earth might endow his servants and others with rewards, in exactly the same way, he endows them precisely in accordance with their initial karmas. And thus, he is not without sovereignty.

Is it not the case that this is not the meaning understood from this verse? What, then, is understood? It is that the Creator alone possesses independence in the assignment of actions to living beings. Whichever action—whether of a violent nature or its opposite—the Creator first assigned to a particular being at the beginning of creation, that being adheres to and performs that very same action. He does not act otherwise by his own will, depending on the instruction of a father or others. Rather, by virtue of the prior decree of Prajāpati, he performs what is good or bad independently, without regard for the instruction of another. Furthermore, "being born again" refers to those being created; Prajāpati himself assigns the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) to their respective roles as agents, either in another kalpa or in this very kalpa. Thus, following that very decree, they perform their former actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious. As it has been said:
"Though they are powerless over their own actions, they assume the state of being agents;
they are impelled by Maheśvara toward that which is auspicious or even inauspicious.
Thus: "This ignorant creature is not master of its own pleasure and pain."
Impelled by the Lord, one may go either to heaven or even into a pit.

It is said in reply: If this were so, the connection between action and its fruit would be abandoned, human effort (puruṣakāra) would become useless, and the injunctions for rites such as the *agnihotra* as well as the meditations on Brahman (*brahmopāsanā*) would result in being rendered purposeless. Only those who are ignorant of the true nature of the Lord would engage in actions for the sake of visible or invisible results. However, for those who consider agency and enjoyment to be dependent upon Him, there would follow a total lack of engagement in any undertaking; even when an action is performed, it would not bear fruit. Furthermore, those who are non-agents might remain indifferent, thinking, "We shall enjoy [the fruits] even though we did not act. Nor does the desire to act arise by force in the wise simply because of the Lord's impulsion, as one might feel toward unwholesome food due to illness. If it is argued that His will is determined by the creation of actions and their fruits—such that from this specific action this particular agency arises—then the principle expressed in the verse "But [He ordains] the action... would not hold. The specific application must be understood solely from the scripture (*śāstra*). Therefore, the Lord first enjoined that person whom He first directed within the beginningless cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), considering the state of being "first" relative to the current existence; and His status as the director over all things follows from His being the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) with respect to space, time, and causal factors.

Others, however, explain it as follows: for a self that has entered another birth, there is no dependence on the conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*) of the previous birth; therefore, its own nature persists. Whatever specific species one was assigned to in a particular action—such as the killing of others—that self, having become of the nature of a lion or other such being, abandons even the gentleness practiced during its human state and adopts the characteristics of its new species, even without being instructed by another. It is thus demonstrated that because actions were performed by Prajāpati, they are powerful by their very nature and cause one who has entered another birth to forget previous habits. (1.28)
He elaborates on this very point:

"The violent and the non-violent, the mild and the cruel, virtue and vice, truth and falsehood—whatever he assigned to each at the beginning of creation, that entered into them of its own accord. (1.29)

*Hiṃsra* (cruel) refers to that which causes the separation of the life-force of others, such as serpents, lions, elephants, and so forth. *Ahiṃsra* (non-cruel) is the opposite of that, such as the *ruru* and *pṛṣata* deer and so forth. *Mṛdu* (gentle) means tender and effortless; *krūra* (cruel) means hard and characterized by the production of suffering for others. The rest is well known. Since this class of action is established in pairs, Prajāpati—having assigned, given, or fashioned each specific action to each being at the beginning of creation (*sarga*), having observed the conformity to their prior karma—that created being enters into and acquires that very action. The past tense is not intended [as a literal historical fact], because even at the beginning of time, it is observed that the characteristics of a species are acquired spontaneously, even though they have not been previously taught. (1.29)
Just as the seasons themselves, at the transition from one season to another, naturally assume their own respective characteristics,
so too do embodied beings undergo their respective actions.

Here is an illustration: just as even insentient things have their own natures established solely by their respective boundaries, so too sentient beings do not transgress the boundaries established by Prajāpati with the assistance of the karma performed by persons; born into whichever class of being they are placed, they perform only that and are unable to do otherwise, even if they so desire.

The seasons are spring and so forth. Their own characteristic marks are the signs such as leaves, fruits, flowers, cold, heat, and rain. Regarding their "succession" (*paryaya*): whichever season has its own succession—that is, the occasion for its own specific function—that season itself undergoes that state; it does not depend upon human effort. For example, mango blossoms bloom by themselves in spring; they do not depend on the sprinkling of water at their roots. In this way, the actions of persons are unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*). There is no object whatsoever that does not depend upon action. To illustrate: the inherent nature of the rains is to bestow rain, yet sometimes a drought occurs due to the fault of the king or the fault of the realm. Therefore, the power of action alone is irremovable. The term "favor" (*anugraha*) is mentioned repeatedly due to the requirements of the meter.
Others, however, explain these three verses differently; they say that by this [passage], the restriction of the inherent nature of the potencies of karma is being stated.

(1.28) That specific ritual action (*karmaviśeṣa*) in which a fruit has been deposited by Prajāpati, when it is repeatedly created and performed, "partakes" in that fruit; the meaning is that it bestows it. By this, it is established that when a sacrifice (*yāga*) has been performed and is about to bear fruit, it does not depend upon anything else at that time. For service (*sevā*), even when performed by oneself, depends on the words of ministers, priests, and so forth; but a sacrifice is not like that. However, a visible operation (*vyāpāra*) is required by it. At that moment, the dependence on another unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*) is precluded, because every effect is produced from a pair of causes, both seen and unseen.

(1.29) Actions that yield desirable and undesirable fruits are the objects of injunctions and prohibitions. He illustrates actions in two ways: "injurious and non-injurious. Injury (*hiṃsā*) is prohibited; its yielding of fruits such as hell is established by the supplementary passages of the Veda, such as: "He who should threaten a Brāhmaṇa, he who should threaten one belonging to me—may he be tormented for a hundred years. That [injury] does not deviate from its inherent nature (*svabhāva*). We shall speak of the specific exceptions regarding expiations (*prāyaścitta*). Non-injury (*ahiṃsra*) is enjoined; even for that, there is no deviation from its inherent nature in terms of yielding desirable fruits. It is only between merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) that there is a distinction. Enjoined action is merit; prohibited action is demerit. Their distinctions include truthfulness, falsehood, and so forth. Truthfulness is enjoined; falsehood is prohibited. In this manner, all the preceding and following terms demonstrate the distinctions between what is enjoined and what is prohibited.
(1.30) Actions whose causal relationship with their effects has been observed to be invariable; the illustration is "like the signs of the seasons. The rest is the same. 1.30.
For the sake of the prosperity of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.

For the sake of the increase of the worlds beginning with the earth—*vṛddhi* meaning growth, nourishment, or abundance. When the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa exist, there is the increase of the three worlds. As it is said: "The gods subsist upon what is given from here" (*TS* 3.2.9.7). And they are those authorized for sacrifice and other rites; therefore, the ritual action performed by them causes both worlds to increase. The gods are impelled by human action. According to the principle, "From the sun rain is born" (*MDh* 3.66), there is also the increase of this world through rain. He brought forth, that is, created, the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa—from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet respectively: from the mouth the Brāhmaṇa, from the two arms the Rājanya, from the two thighs the Vaiśya, and from the feet the Śūdra. The suffix *tasiḥ* is used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*) according to Pāṇini 5.4.45. It is as if the effect were extracted from the cause; when there is a separation, there is the status of the ablative. He fashioned some primordial Brāhmaṇa from the parts of his own mouth by means of divine power, because we observe that all present-day beings are produced from their constituent elements (*tattva*) through the medium of sexual union. In the highest sense, this is a figurative praise intended to demonstrate the relative excellence and inferiority of the castes. Prajāpati is the best of all beings; of him, too, the mouth is the best among all limbs. Likewise, the Brāhmaṇa is the most praiseworthy of all castes. On this basis of similarity, he is said to have been produced from the mouth of Brahmā. Or rather, he is said to be "from the mouth" because of the preeminence of the mouth's functions, such as teaching and so forth. For the Kṣatriya, too, the function of the arms is warfare. For the Vaiśya, the function of the thighs is tending cattle—wandering where cows graze—or traveling via land and water routes for the sake of trade. For the Śūdra, the function of the feet is service. (1.31)
Dividing his own body into two parts, he became a man with one half and a woman with the other; in her, the Lord created Virāj.

This creation is directly from the Supreme Person; others, however, say that this [creation] belongs to that very Brahmā. Having divided that body which had emerged within the egg into two parts, with one half he became a male person (*puruṣa*), a man capable of emitting semen; with the other half, a woman, in the manner of Gaurī and Śiva. Or rather, he fashioned her as something entirely separate. Having fashioned her, through the act of sexual union, he generated him whose name is well-known as Virāj. This is what is meant: "Prajāpati went unto his own daughter. Even this statement regarding the division into two is based on the fact that the bodies of husband and wife differ only in form, while they remain inseparable in all their functions. (1.32)
O best of the twice-born, know me to be that Virāj, the Supreme Person, whom he himself created after performing austerities; I am the creator of all this.

Know me to be that Puruṣa whom Virāṭ, having performed austerities, created. Thus, through this tradition of memory, there is nothing concerning me that remains unknown to you which needs to be described here. In the midst of this, he declares his own purity: [he is] the creator of all this. By this, he expresses his omnipotence. The intention is that he will cause me—who possess an excellence of birth and deeds—to be trusted; and for the sake of producing certainty, because he mentions his own human birth even though it is already known from other sources. Just as someone who has heard of one’s status from another might be asked, “Are you the son of Devadatta? and when he replies, “Indeed,” certainty arises. For poets, the description of one’s lineage is a source of shame, even when it constitutes self-praise through traditional succession. “O best of the twice-born” is the address. “Sattamāḥ” means the most virtuous, the most excellent. (1.33)
Desiring to create progeny, I performed most difficult austerities and first created ten great seers as the lords of creatures.

I created—that is, I brought forth—the ten Prajāpatis, the great seers (maharṣis), after first performing asceticism that was exceedingly difficult to practice; for it is performed with great pain, being most oppressive and enduring for a long time. || 1.34 ||
He names those great seers [82]:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada. (1.35)
These [Manus], possessing immense splendor, created seven other Manus, as well as the gods, the hosts of gods, and the great seers of immeasurable power. (1.36)

These seven great seers (maharṣis) created other Manus. This word "Manu" denotes a specific office (*adhikāra*): he who, during a Manvantara, possesses authority over the creation or the maintenance of progeny in the manner described is called a Manu. The terms *bhūritejasaḥ* ("of abundant splendor") and *amitaujasaḥ* ("of immeasurable power") have the same meaning. One [term], ending in the nominative case, is an attribute of the Creator; the second, ending in the accusative case, is an attribute of those to be created, such as the Manus and others. [Objection: But were not the gods already created by Brahmā? [Reply: True, but not all of them. For the hosts of gods are infinite. The "assemblies of gods" (*devanikāya*) are the abodes of the gods, such as the heavenly worlds (*svargaloka*), the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), and so forth. (1.36)
And the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas; the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Asuras; the Nāgas, Sarpas, and Suparṇas; and the various hosts of the Pitṛs. || 1.37 ||

The specific nature of the yakṣas and other beings is established solely by means of traditional accounts (*aitihya*) and the like; it is not determined by any of the other means of valid cognition, such as direct perception. Among them, the *yakṣas* are the followers of Vaiśravaṇa. The *rākṣasas* include Vibhīṣaṇa and others. The *piśācas* are more cruel than those; they dwell in impure places, deserts, and similar regions, and are inferior to the *yakṣas* and *rākṣasas*. However, all of them are indeed harmful. According to historians and practitioners of mantras, some of them, by employing deception, draw away the life-force of living beings through an invisible power and produce diseases. The *gandharvas* are the attendants of the gods, preeminent in song and dance. The *apsarases* are the courtesans of the gods, such as Urvaśī and others. The *asuras* are the enemies of the gods, including Vṛtra, Virocana, Hiraṇyākṣa, and so forth. The *nāgas* include Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and others. The *sarpas* (serpents) are well known. The *suparṇas* are a particular class of birds, such as Garuḍa and others. The *pitṛs* (ancestors) have names such as Somapās and Ājyapās; they abide in their own realm like gods. He created their host. (1.37)
Lightnings, thunderclouds, and red clouds; rainbows of Indra;
meteors, thunderclaps, and comets; and celestial lights of various kinds.

Light visible within the belly of clouds is called lightning (*vidyut*). Its synonyms, such as *taḍit* and *saudāminī*, are based on its specific characteristics. When it becomes solidified like stone, it is called a thunderbolt (*aśani*). When it falls like raindrops or streams of water, being driven by powerful winds and destroying crops and the like, it is so designated. Clouds (*megha*) are atmospheric masses consisting of water, wind, and light. A red phenomenon (*rohita*) shaped like a staff, appearing blue and red in color, is sometimes seen in the sky; sometimes it is attached to the solar disc, and sometimes it appears in other regions. A specific variety of this is the rainbow (*indradhanus*), which possesses a greater degree of curvature and the shape of a bow. Meteors (*ulkā*) are those luminous bodies seen falling in all directions during portents, such as at twilight or dusk, emitting spreading rays of light. A thunderclap (*nirghāta*) is a portentous sound arising from the earth or the atmosphere. Comets (*ketu*) are well-known luminous bodies with crests that appear during portents. There are also various other types, such as Dhruva, Agastya, Arundhatī, and so forth. (1.38)
Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, and various birds;
domestic animals, wild beasts, humans, and fanged predators.

Those creatures with horse-faces who dwell on the Himavat and other mountains are the *kiṃnaras*. Monkeys have the faces of apes and the bodies of humans. Birds are winged creatures. Cattle include goats, sheep, camels, donkeys, and so forth. Deer include the *ruru*, the *pṛṣata*, and others. Beasts of prey include lions, tigers, and so forth. Those which possess two rows of teeth, one above and one below, are called "those with teeth on both sides" (*ubhayatodan*). (1.39)
And worms, insects, and moths; lice, flies, and bugs; all gadflies and mosquitoes; and various kinds of stationary beings. 1.40.

Worms (*kṛmi*) are extremely minute living beings. Insects (*kīṭa*) are slightly larger than those and move upon the earth. Moths (*pataṅga*) include locusts, winged insects, and the like. "Immovable things" (*sthāvara*) refers to trees, mountains, and so forth. "Various kinds" (*pṛthagvidha*) means of many sorts. The term "small creatures" (*kṣudrajantu*) is treated as a singular collective. (1.40)
Thus, by my command, all this— both the stationary and the moving— was created by those great-souled ones through the application of their ascetic power, each according to their own karma.

"Thus" (*evam*) refers back to the manner previously described [in verse 40]. By these great-souled ones, Marīci and the others, all this—both the stationary and the moving—was created. "According to their karma" (*yathākarma*) means in dependence upon whatever kind of karma was performed by each in a previous birth. Furthermore, whichever species of birth it was appropriate for a being to arise in due to the power of their karma, they were produced in that very species. "By my command" (*manniyogāt*) means by my order. "Through the application of austerity" (*tapoyogāt*) means having performed great austerity; by this he says that whatever great sovereignty there may be, all of that is to be attained through austerity. (1.41)
I shall describe to you, according to their respective order, what kind of karma has been proclaimed for each of these beings here, as well as the sequence of their births.

For those beings, whatever their action is—whether by nature harmful or non-harmful—it has been described accordingly. Now, I shall explain the application of the order of birth. But where was the action described, since in this [list] beginning with "yakṣas" and "rakṣas," there is a designation of names and not a designation of actions? It is said: the understanding of the action follows precisely from the designation of the name, because the acquisition of these names is based upon that action. For instance: they are *yakṣas* because of *yakṣaṇa* (devouring), *bhakṣaṇa* (eating), or *aśana* (consuming); *rakṣasas* because of destroying (*kṣaṇana*) in secret; *piśācas* because of eating flesh (*piśita*); *apsarases* because they flowed forth from the waters (*adbhyaḥ sṛtāḥ*); *asuras* because of the failure to obtain the liquor called *amṛta*; and so on should be inferred for others as well. Regarding the order of birth, the sequence beginning with "viviparous" (*jarāyuja*) and "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*) will be explained [in the following verse]. 1.42.
Domestic animals, wild beasts, and carnivorous predators with two rows of teeth;
Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and humans—all are born from the womb. (1.43)

These are the viviparous (*jarāyuja*). *Jarāyu* is the membrane, the bed of the embryo; therein they first come into being, and thereafter, having been released, they are born. This is their order of birth. Since there is another word *dat* which has the same meaning as the word *danta*, the form *ubhayatodataḥ* is appropriate in the nominative plural. 1.43.
Birds born from eggs, snakes, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises— whatever other such creatures there are, whether terrestrial or aquatic.

Crocodiles, porpoises, and the like; the tortoise, which is a *kūrma*; and those of this same kind, such as lizards and others that dwell on land; likewise, aquatic creatures born in water, such as conches and the like. (1.44)
Gnats, mosquitoes, lice, flies, and bugs are born from moisture, as are whatever other such things there may be. (1.45)

Sweat is the internal moisture of earthly substances arising from contact with the heat of fire, the sun, and so forth; from that, gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like are born. Furthermore, whatever else is of this nature—extremely minute creatures such as gnats and ants—that is produced by warmth. Warmth is indeed sweat, or rather, heat is its cause. Alternatively, the reading may be "upajāyante" (they are produced). One should read: "And whatever others are of this kind. (1.45)
All stationary beings are born from sprouts; they grow from seeds or from stems.
Herbs are those that perish after the ripening of their fruit and are endowed with many flowers and fruits. (1.46)

*Udbhid* means that which breaks forth; the suffix *kvip* is used here in the sense of an action (*bhāve*). Those which are born from this are called *udbhijjāḥ*. Trees are born by breaking through and splitting open the sown seed and the earth. All [plants] sprout and grow from seeds and stems, becoming firm with roots, trunks, and so forth. The same applies to herbs (*oṣadhyaḥ*). "Herbs" (*oṣadhayaḥ*) is the correct form; the long vowel *ī* is either according to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ* or is Vedic (*chāndasa*). This is their natural function: they end with ripening, meaning their end or destruction occurs when the fruit has ripened. Once the fruit is ripe, rice and other grains perish, yet they become endowed with many flowers and fruits. This qualification applies to both herbs and trees as far as applicable. (1.46)
Those which bear fruit without flowers are known as *vanaspatis*;
those that bear both flowers and fruit are known as *vṛkṣas*. || 1.47 ||

Those which produce fruit without flowers are called *vanaspatis*, not *vṛkṣas*. Those that possess both flowers and fruit are *vṛkṣas*. Due to the occurrence of both [characteristics], in some cases *vanaspatis* are also called *vṛkṣas*, and *vṛkṣas* are also called *vanaspatis*. We shall demonstrate the specific reason for this distinction later.

We, however, say this: this is not an injunction regarding the relationship between words and their meanings, as is the case with the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*). Therefore, the meaning is not that those things which possess such a nature are denoted by the word *vanaspati* and so forth; rather, the birth of flowers and fruits is being stated. For that [birth] is the subject under discussion, as in the verse: "But [I shall describe] the order and connection in [their] birth" (MDh 1.42). The production of fruits is twofold: they are produced without flowers, and from flowers. Likewise, flowers are produced from trees. Thus, although the designation is such that "those which bear fruit are to be known as *vanaspatis*," nevertheless, by the force of the context, an exchange of the relative pronoun (*yat*) and the demonstrative pronoun (*tat*) must be made. That is to say: those well-known as *vanaspatis* are those which bear fruit without flowers; from them, fruits are produced without flowers. And by the force of the context, this sequence is established. Just as in the expression "wrap the pillar with a cloth," when the cloth is to be wrapped, the meaning becomes: "having placed the cloth around the pillar, cause it to be wrapped. This [verse] is restated even though it is already well-known, in order to establish the point made in the verse: "by means of manifold darkness" (MDh 1.49). || 1.47 ||

Furthermore, there are various kinds of shrubs and clusters, as well as species of grasses; likewise, there are those that grow from seeds and from stems, as well as spreading creepers and climbing vines.

Those creepers that grow from the earth in clusters, whether with a single root or many roots, and do not attain great growth—their aggregate is designated by the terms *guccha* and *gulma*, such as *tṛṇamūlaka* and the like. The distinction between these two is based on whether they have flowers or lack them. Or there are other species of grasses, such as *kuśa*, *śādvala*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, and so forth. *Pratāna* refers to long, ground-reaching shoots of grass. *Vallī* and *vratatī* are those which, having sprung up from the earth, wind around a tree or some other object and climb upwards. All of this, like trees, grows from seeds or from slips. (1.48)
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions,
these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.

They are enveloped—that is, pervaded—by that *tamas* whose cause is karma known as *adharma*. This *tamas* is multiform, serving as the occasion for the experience of various sufferings. Although everything consists of the three *guṇas*, nevertheless, in these beings *tamas* is predominant, while *sattva* and *rajas* are diminished. Therefore, due to the abundance of *tamas*, they remain for a very long time experiencing the fruit of unrighteousness, constantly joined with despondency, suffering, and the like. Yet, because *sattva* also exists there, they enjoy even a slight trace of pleasure in certain states. Thus it is said: "endowed with pleasure and pain. Regarding the term "internal consciousness" (*antaḥsaṃjñā*): *saṃjñā* is the intellect (*buddhi*). They are called "internally conscious" because of the absence of external activities such as movement or speech, which are the effects and manifestations of that [intellect]. Otherwise, every person would be conscious only internally. Alternatively, unlike humans who first perceive the prick of a thorn and so forth, immobile beings do not perceive in this way; they require a great stimulus, such as being split by an axe, to have the perception of suffering, just like living beings in states of sleep, intoxication, or fainting. (1.49)
These states of existence, beginning with Brahmā, are declared to end here within this terrible cycle of birth for beings, which is eternal and ever-moving.

This is the end, the finality; those courses of existence whose limit is this are "ending with this. The connection of the self with various bodies for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of performed actions is called a "course" (*gati*). There is no other course lower than this state of being stationary, nor is there any course superior to the attainment of Brahman, which consists of bliss. These courses are attained through auspicious and inauspicious actions known as *dharma* and *adharma*. However, the attainment of the Supreme Brahman—which is characterized by liberation and consists of absolute bliss—comes from knowledge, or from the combination of knowledge and action, as we shall explain later.

In the *bhūtasaṃsāra*—the cycle of existence for beings (*bhūta*), that is, for the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*)—which is a continuous succession of birth and death, the transition into other states of being; which is *ghora*, terrifying to those possessed of negligence and laziness due to the arising of separation from the beloved and union with the unloved; which is characterized by constant movement at all times, perishable, and though essence-less, eternally *ghora* (never indeed *aghora*); and which remains *ghora* even when one stays for a very long time in the destinies of gods and so forth, because one must eventually die—it is thus, by this description of the cycle of existence as having merit and demerit as its cause, that the great purpose of the treatise is established. For, through the treatise, there arises the knowledge of the discrimination between merit and demerit; therefore, it should be studied. (1.50)
Having thus created all this and me as well, he of inconceivable prowess again withdrew himself into his own self, subduing time with time.

Thus, having created and produced this entire world—partly directly and partly by the command of Prajāpati—and having appointed me to the maintenance of the world, that Blessed One, whose power, prowess, and capacity regarding all objects are inconceivable, wonderful, and great, vanished after creation; that is, he made himself invisible, casting off the body assumed at will through the power of yoga and becoming once more unmanifest. Regarding the word *ātmani* (in himself): it is not as other entities vanish into primordial nature (*prakṛti*), for he does not vanish elsewhere. Rather, he is dissolved in himself alone, because there is no other primordial nature for him into which he could vanish, since he is the primordial nature of all beings. Alternatively, "vanishing" means the cessation of all worldly activities. The present participle (*sṛjan*, "creating") should be understood as referring to the action of "having created" (*sṛṣṭvā*). He destroys the time of dissolution by means of the time of creation and maintenance. "Again" (*bhūyaḥ*) means "once more. As he will say: "Creations and dissolutions are infinite" (1.27). 1.51.
When that God is awake, the world thus moves;
when He, whose self is tranquil, sleeps, then everything closes its eyes.

When that deity awakens—that is, when he desires, "Let this world be produced; let it attain this state and endure for such a length of time"—then it becomes active. It becomes endowed with mental, vocal, and physical operations, both internal and external, such as inhalation and exhalation, eating, moving about, agriculture, sacrifice, and so forth. When he sleeps—that is, when his desire for the creation and maintenance of the world ceases—then everything closes its eyes and undergoes dissolution. The waking and sleeping of Prajāpati are said to be the engagement in and the withdrawal from activity according to his will. His state of tranquility is the reabsorption of the state of differentiation. (1.52)
But when that Lord, established in his own nature, sleeps, the embodied beings whose essence is action desist from their respective activities,
and the mind falls into exhaustion.

This verse, which follows the previous explanation, has a clear meaning. "Svasthe" means well-established or stable. "Śāntātmavat" means like one whose nature is pure. "Abiding in one's own self" (*svātmany avasthānam*) is the cessation of distinctions caused by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*). "Karmātmānaḥ" refers to those for whom action is primary—the transmigrating individual souls (*kṣetrajña*). They are called "embodied beings" (*śarīriṇaḥ*) because they experience a connection with a body through their connection with karma; it is in this sense that they are so described. While He sleeps, they cease from their respective activities. By this, the cessation of bodily movement is expressed. "And the mind reaches exhaustion" (*manaś ca glānim ṛcchati*); by this, the cessation of internal activity is indicated. Thus, through the cessation of both external and internal activity, dissolution (*pralaya*) is established. "Exhaustion" (*glāni*) is a lack of enthusiasm; it "reaches" or attains a state of incapacity regarding its own functions. (1.53)
But when they dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self,
then this Self of all beings sleeps happily and in peace.

This verse should be explained by reversing the relative positions of "yat" and "tat"; otherwise, with respect to the preceding verse, a circular dependency would result. This is what is meant: when he sleeps, then everything closes its eyes.

He sleeps happily, at peace. The Supreme Brahman is the very nature of bliss; for him there is no happiness in the state of sleep and no suffering at other times. And his sleep is exactly as previously described. His peace (*nirvṛti*) exists at all times, for that Supreme Self is not touched by the waves of the affliction of ignorance (*avidyā*); he consists solely of bliss. His agency over the entire universe is thus established. Just as this man, having ceased from household duties, sleeps happily and at ease—thinking, "I have accomplished what was to be done, the wealth acquired is useful for the home, and I have become free from trouble"—and being thus peaceful and free from any fear of injury to himself, so too is He compared. This praise is offered because this entire world is His family.

Alternatively, this verse should be explained as referring to *pradhāna* (the primordial matter). In that case, *pradhāna* "sleeps" when all beings simultaneously dissolve into it, attaining its own nature—that is, the state of the cause—and emerge from their state of modification, as many as exist within the belly of the three worlds. Furthermore, sleep is the cessation of transformation, not the withdrawal of cognition, because *pradhāna* is insentient. And "bliss" is used figuratively for the very same reason of its insentiency. (1.54)
But having resorted to this darkness, he remains for a long time endowed with the senses;
yet he does not perform his own action, and then he departs from his bodily form.

Now, the death of the transmigrating person and the attainment of another body are described by these two verses. "Darkness" (*tamas*) is the cessation of knowledge; having resorted to that, he remains for a long time, staying with his senses. Yet he does not perform his own functions, such as inhalation and exhalation. Then he departs—that is, he goes—out from the embodied form, the physical body.
But surely, the Self is all-pervading and omnipresent like space; what kind of departure can it have?

Departure (*utkrānti*) is simply the relinquishing of the body acquired through karma; it is not, however, the movement of a material object from one place to another. Alternatively, some maintain that there exists another subtle body called the *antarābhava* (intermediate state), of which this departure is the exit. Others, however, do not accept the existence of an intermediate body. As the venerable Vyāsa said: "O King, when this body has passed away, the sense faculties simply abide in another body; therefore, there is no intermediate state."

Even among the Sāṃkhyas, some such as Vindhyavāsin and others do not accept the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). What is this so-called intermediate state? When this body has perished, but before one has reached the destination—such as the mother’s womb—for the sake of taking up a second body, there arises in the interval a subtle body devoid of sensory enjoyment. It is such that it has no contact with anything, is not burned by fire and the like, and is not obstructed by the gross elements (*mahābhūta*). Others, however, speak of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as having form; they say that the Supreme Self, whose nature is the soul of all, stands like the ocean, and from it the individual souls (*jīva*) emerge, falling into a state of differentiation due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), just like waves from the great sea. As that [Self] emerges from there, a subtle body called the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) is accepted as its mark (*liṅga*). By virtue of previously performed merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), it is the subtle body that serves as the dwelling place for each individual soul. As it is stated in the Purāṇa:
He is joined with the subtle body (liṅga), known as the vital breath (prāṇa), consisting of the eightfold city;
for one bound by it there is bondage, and for one liberated from it there is liberation.

These five—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—together with the group of the five sense organs, the group of the five organs of action, and the mind as the eighth, constitute the *puryaṣṭaka* (the city of eight). That body does not perish until the state of liberation (*mokṣa*). Thus it has been said: "The subtle body (*liṅga*), permeated by dispositions, transmigrates through states devoid of [gross] experience. (1.55)
When, having become as minute as an atom, he enters, conjoined with it, the seed—whether stationary or moving—then he casts off his form. (1.56)

That which has subtle (*aṇvyaḥ*) parts—that is, minute components—is called *aṇumātrika*. This refers either to the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), or the selves (*ātman*) themselves, which are subtle by their very nature. As it is said: "This very self within the heart is smaller than a grain," and so forth (ChU 3.14.3). The seed is the cause for the production of a body; the stationary is that which is the cause for the birth of trees and the like; the moving is that which is locomotive. It enters, presides over, and becomes bound [to these]. When it is conjoined with those [elements] such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), then it releases its [prior] form and binds itself; the meaning is that it takes on a body. (1.56)
Thus, through waking and dreaming, that imperishable one incessantly brings this entire world of moving and non-moving beings to life and causes it to perish.

This is a summary of what was previously stated: by means of waking and dreaming, which are connected to the Self, He gives life to and causes the death of the world—both the moving and the non-moving, the stationary and the wandering. He is imperishable and indestructible. (1.57)
Having composed this treatise himself, he first caused me alone to receive it according to the prescribed rule; I, in turn, [taught] the sages beginning with Marīci.

Here, by the word "śāstra" (treatise), the collection of Smṛti injunctions and prohibitions is meant, and not the physical book, because that was composed by Manu. For this reason, it is designated as "Mānava" (the work of Manu); otherwise, it would have been designated as "Hairaṇyagarbha" (the work of Hiraṇyagarbha).

However, some maintain that even though the work was originally composed by Hiraṇyagarbha, its designation as "Mānava" (belonging to Manu) is entirely appropriate because it was elucidated by Manu for many people. Just as the Gaṅgā, though first discovered on the Himavat mountains, is designated as "Haimavatī" (born of the Himavat) despite having originated elsewhere; and just as the *Pravacana* known as the *Kāṭhaka* is designated after Kaṭha because it is constantly studied by him—despite there being other students and teachers—the designation is made after Kaṭha due to his excellence in teaching. Moreover, Nārada records: "This work consists of one hundred thousand verses and was composed by Prajāpati; from that, it was gradually abridged by Manu and others. Therefore, even if it were composed by another, the designation "Mānava" is not contradictory. Furthermore, the use of the word *śāstra* to denote a book is indeed observed, since it conveys the sense of being an instruction (*śāsana*).

"He caused me alone to grasp [it]," meaning "I was taught by him. By these words—"himself," "from the beginning," and "according to rule"—the non-destruction of the tradition (*āgama*) is expressed. For when an author himself teaches his own work for the first time, not even a single syllable (*mātrā*) is lost therein. However, for another who has acquired it from that [author] and is teaching it to someone else, there is no effort toward the preservation of that work. Even for the author, having previously taught it, one might suspect a lapse due to negligence or laziness on the second occasion, thinking, "This work was previously established by me. Therefore, it is said "from the beginning. "According to rule" (*vidhivat*): "rule" (*vidhi*) refers to the focused state of mind and qualities such as undistracted attention on the part of both student and teacher. The suffix *-vati* is used in the sense of fitness (*arhe*), according to Pāṇini 5.1.117.

"But as for the sages Marīci and the others"—Marīci and the rest are of well-known power; by showing that even they studied this [work] from my presence, he demonstrates his own status as a teacher through his connection with distinguished disciples. Furthermore, by means of the greatness of the scripture of the great seers, he generates an excess of faith so that there may be no cessation of study. "This great scripture is of such a kind that it was studied even by Marīci and the others, and Manu, such a great soul, is their teacher"—thus, thinking "it is fitting to study this text from his presence," the listeners do not desist until the completion of the scripture. In both ways, therefore, this is a praise of the scripture. (1.58)
This Bhṛgu will proclaim this scripture to you in its entirety;
for this sage has learned all of this from me without exception.

This scripture—this entire work—he, Bhrigu, will cause you to hear in its entirety; he will bring it to the path of your ears, teach it, and explain it. This is the concluding reflection on this scripture. The sage learned this entire, complete scripture from me—from my presence (*mattaḥ*). Since knowledge seems to emerge from the mouth of the teacher and the disciple seems to receive it, the use of the ablative suffix *tas* in "from me" (*mattaḥ*) is appropriate to denote the source. Bhrigu, however, is of most renowned power among the great seers. By appointing him as the expounder, it is demonstrated that this scripture has come down through a lineage of transmission from many who possessed various, complete, and unsurpassed sciences. And for this reason, there is seen even this mode of engagement in some: "This scripture has descended from many great souls; why should we not study it? Thus, an inclination toward the study and practice of the scripture is generated. (1.59)
Then, having been addressed in that manner by Manu, the great seer Bhṛgu, with a joyful soul, spoke to all those sages: "Let it be heard! (1.60)

That great seer Bhṛgu, having been addressed thus by Manu—"He shall proclaim this to you"—and being appointed immediately thereafter, spoke to those seers: "Listen! With a joyful heart in the presence of his many disciples, he said, "I have been appointed here. Through this great honor, his heart was filled with joy; for, by virtue of his fitness as a speaker, Bhṛgu felt great respect for himself, thinking, "I have been esteemed by him as one who carries out his commands. (1.60)
Of this Svāyaṃbhuva Manu, there were six other high-souled and immensely powerful Manus belonging to his lineage, who each created their own respective progeny.

The Preceptor (Upādhyāya), being questioned regarding the origin of the world and other matters, has described them. In the same manner, the Disciple (Śiṣya), having been appointed by him, has begun to describe the remainder of that very subject. By the word "asya" (of this), he refers directly to Manu. Of our Preceptor, who is known as Svāyaṃbhuva, there are six other Manus who are his *vaṃśyas*—that is, born in the same lineage or family (*vaṃśa*). All of them are called *vaṃśyas* because they were all created directly by Brahmā and thus originate from a single family. Alternatively, those authorized for a single task are called *vaṃśyas*; for the designation "lineage" (*vaṃśa*) among living beings arises through the connection to a single function. As in the expression: "Two sages are the *vaṃśyas* of grammar. And he shows that one single Dharma: "They created their own respective subjects. In each Manvantara, whichever Manu holds authority is the creator and protector of the subjects destroyed in the preceding Manvantara. Therefore, whatever subjects are created by a particular Manu, they become his "own" (*svāḥ*). (1.61)
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and the son of Vivasvat as well.

He points out those Manus by name. "Mahātejāḥ" (of great splendor) is an epithet; the other names are either conventional (*rūḍhi*) or based on etymological composition (*nibandha*). "Vivasvatsutaḥ" (the son of Vivasvat) is a distinct word formed as a compound, like words such as *kṛṣṇasarpa* (black snake) or *narasiṃha* (man-lion). || 1.62 ||
These seven Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possessed immense splendor;
each, within his own interval, produced and sustained this entire world of moving and non-moving beings.

Here, seven Manus have been described by me; elsewhere, fourteen are accounted for. "In their respective intervals" (antare) means when their time of authority has arrived—that is to say, having produced progeny, they protected them. "In their respective intervals" refers to the period of authority for each Manu, at whatever time the mandate for creation, maintenance, and protection was attained by that particular Manu. Others, however, consider the word *antara* to denote a specific duration of time, like the words "month" and so forth. That is incorrect; the term *manvantara* is a specific period of time designated as such only when conjoined with the word *manu*, and not by itself. (1.63)
Eighteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, thirty of those make one *kalā*, thirty *kalās* make one *muhūrta*, and a day and night (*ahorātra*) consists of as many [muhūrtas]. (1.64)

In order to define the measure of time for the duration of the world's persistence and its dissolution, he begins to explain the divisions of time as they fall within the scope of the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*). Eighteen *nimeṣas* constitute a unit of time called a *kāṣṭhā*. Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are a *kalā*. Thirty *kalās* would be one *muhūrta*; the meaning is that thirty of those [units]. Thirty *muhūrtas* are a day and night (*ahorātra*). Having supplied the verb "one should know" (*vidyāt*), the word "those many" (*tāvat*) is in the accusative plural. Now, what is this so-called *nimeṣa*? It is the natural blinking of the eyelids, which accompanies the opening of the eyes. However, others have stated that a *nimeṣa* is the amount of time in which an unmodified syllable is pronounced. (1.64)
The sun divides day and night for both human beings and gods:
night is for the sleep of living beings, and day is for the performance of actions.

Day and night constitute *ahorātra*. The sun effects their division: as long as the sun has risen and its rays are visible, there is the conventional usage of "day"; once it has set, until its next rising, there is the conventional usage of "night," whether in the world of humans or the world of the gods. But how is this division of day and night to be understood in places where the sun does not reach with its rays? To this he says: "Night is for sleep. Among beings that are self-luminous, because they are eternally illuminated, the division [between day and night] occurs through activity and exertion on the one hand, and through sleep on the other. Just as the time of the manifestation of medicinal herbs is fixed by their very nature, so too activity, exertion, and sleep are fixed by the nature of time itself. (1.65)
For the ancestors, a month constitutes a day and a night, divided into two fortnights;
the dark fortnight is their day for active duties, and the bright fortnight is their night for sleep. (1.66)

That which is a month for humans is a day and night for the ancestors (*pitṛs*). What is the division as to which is the day and which is the night? This is the distinction: "this is the day" and "this is the night. This division is established within the two fortnights (*pakṣa*) known as half-months, which consist of fifteen nights each; the meaning is that it is dependent upon the fortnights. One fortnight is the day and the other is the night; and because these two possess distinct natures and a fixed sequence, he states their specific difference: the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is the day, and the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) is the night. The reading "from ritual activities" (*karmaceṣṭābhyaḥ*) is appropriate, just as in the case of "for sleep" (*svapnāya*); it is precisely the state of being for the sake of that [activity] which is intended here as the object. The locative case is used here due to metrical requirements. (1.66)
For the gods, a year consists of night and day; their division is as follows:
the northern course (udagayana) is their day, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is their night. 1.67.

A year for humans—consisting of twelve months—is a single day and night for the gods. Furthermore, there is a division of that [year] by means of the northern course (*udagayana*) and the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*). Among these, for the sun as it sets out toward the northern direction, there is the northern course lasting six months. "Course" (*ayana*) means going or abiding. During those six months, the sun rises in that [northern] direction. Then, for the sun that has turned back, there is the southern course; for, having moved toward the southern direction and abandoned the north, it causes its rising. (1.67)
Now learn, in brief, the measure of a day and night of Brahmā, and the duration of each of the Yugas in their proper order. 1.68.

Brahmā is the creator of progeny; listen from me, in brief and concisely, regarding the measure of his world—the duration of its nights and days (ahorātra) and of the yugas—individually for each yuga.

This verse is intended to state the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) of the section about to be discussed, in order to secure the attention of the listeners; hence the address, "Listen! (*nibodhata*). Furthermore, the restatement regarding the division of time under discussion is for the purpose of indicating that this is a distinct section. Consequently, the matter to be explained is not merely a supplement to the beginning of the treatise, but pertains to *dharma* as well. Thus he will say: "They know the day of Brahmā to be meritorious" (MDh 1.73). The meaning is that merit arises from the knowledge thereof. (1.68)
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
Because they are the subject under discussion, the divine years (*divyavarṣa*) are understood here. And so says the author of the Purāṇa:
"O twice-born ones, this has been sung by the sages according to the divine reckoning;
the number of the *yugas* is proclaimed by means of the divine measure alone."

Those four thousand [years] constitute the period known as the Kṛtayuga. The twilight (saṃdhyā) of that Kṛtayuga consists of exactly as many hundreds—four hundred. Its "twilight-part" (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same kind and the same measure; that is to say, it consists of four hundred years. That period wherein there is a persistence of the nature of both the past and the future time is the twilight (saṃdhyā). The twilight-part (saṃdhyāṃśa) is the conformity to the characteristics of both times, wherein there is a slight persistence of the qualities of the previous age and a greater persistence of those of the age yet to come. (1.69)
In the other three [ages], together with their twilights and twilight-portions,
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.

In the three ages other than the Kṛtayuga—namely the Tretā and the others—along with their respective junctions (sandhyā) and sub-junctions (sandhyāṃśa), there occurs a decline or diminution. In the Tretā, there is a loss of one thousand years compared to the Kṛtayuga; likewise from the Tretā to the Dvāpara, and from the Dvāpara to the Kali. Thus, it becomes three thousand years for the Tretā, two for the Dvāpara, and one for the Kali. In the junctions and their sub-junctions, hundreds of years are diminished. A specific collection of days is called a "yuga," and its particular divisions are the Kṛta and the others.

The vowel *ī* in the word “tāvacchatī” should be remembered. Here, it means “smṛti” (tradition). It is the collection (*samāhāra*) of so many hundreds. Since the word “tāvat” ends in the suffix *vat* according to Pāṇini 1.1.23, it receives the designation of a numeral (*saṃkhyā*). When the designation of a *dvigu* compound applies by Pāṇini 2.1.52, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by Pāṇini 4.1.21 as an exception to the suffix *ṭāp*. [The analysis is: “that of which the measure (*parimāṇa*) is a hundred. The suffix *vatup* is added by Pāṇini 5.2.39, and the vowel *ā* is substituted by Pāṇini 6.3.91. Otherwise, if it were a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning “she who has so many hundreds”—then because the word “śata” ends in *ā*, the suffix *ṭāp* would have to be applied by Pāṇini 4.1.4. If that were done, the form would be “tāvacchatā”; this is the intended meaning. || 1.70 ||
This cycle of four ages (caturyuga) which has been enumerated at the very beginning consists of twelve thousand [years]; this is called a yuga of the gods.

The phrase "this which" (*yad etad*) is a common worldly expression used to refer back to a subject previously introduced as a whole. This refers to the four ages (*caturyuga*) whose number has been determined at the beginning—prior to this verse—by such statements as "four thousand [years]," and so forth. Regarding this four-age cycle (*caturyuga*), twelve thousand [of these] are called a *yuga* of the gods (*devānāṃ yugam*). The meaning is that a period of time consisting of twelve thousand four-age cycles is named a "divine age" (*devayuga*). The suffix *aṇ* is applied here in its own sense (without changing the meaning) after the word *sahasra*. The analysis of the compound is: "that in which the measure is twelve thousand four-age cycles. (1.71)
A thousand divine yugas, by calculation, should be known as one day of Brahmā; his night is of exactly the same duration.

A thousand divine yugas constitute one day of Brahmā; his night is of the same duration, namely a thousand divine yugas. The connection is with "thousand" (*sahasram*) by way of enumeration (*parisaṃkhyayā*) or calculation (*saṃkhyānena*). This restatement is for the purpose of completing the verse, for the conventional usage of "thousand" and so forth does not occur without a specific number. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of cause (*hetau*). (1.72)
Those people who know day and night truly understand that the holy day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas, and his night is of exactly the same duration. 1.73.

That whose end is a thousand yugas is "that which ends after a thousand yugas" (yugasahasrānta). Those humans who know this are "knowers of day and night. When the question arises as to what happens to them, the connection is that "merit accrues [to them]. Since knowing the measure of a day of Brahmā is meritorious, one should therefore understand it; thus, through this praise, there is an injunction for its practice. (1.73)
At the end of that night, he who has been sleeping awakens;
having awakened, he creates the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.

That Brahmā, having experienced sleep during that long night, awakens; thereafter, he creates the world again. His sleep is of the nature already described; for he does not sleep like an ordinary person, owing to his eternal wakefulness. Regarding this, he states the sequence of creation: "The mind, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent. Now, it was previously stated: "In the beginning, he created the waters alone" (MDh 1.8). Some say that dissolution is of two kinds: the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) and the intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*). This sequence applies to the intermediate dissolution. Furthermore, in this context, the "mind" (*manas*) is not one of the [twenty-four] principles (*tattva*), because it had already arisen previously. What then? The meaning is that the awakened Prajāpati creates and directs the mind for the purpose of further creation. However, in the second case—that of the great dissolution—the mind would be the principle of "the Great One" (*mahat-tattva*) because it is the cause of the mind, and thus there would be a contradiction with the previously stated sequence. For it is said in the Purāṇa:
"Mind (manas), the Great One (mahat), intellect (mati), awakening (buddhi), and greatness (mahattva) are proclaimed; these words are celebrated as synonyms for the Great One. (1.74)
The mind, impelled by the desire to create, undergoes transformation and brings forth the creation;
from that, space is born, and they know sound to be its quality. (1.75)

Although this creation of reality has already been described, it is stated once more in order to establish those specific details that were not previously mentioned. Being impelled by Brahman, it undergoes transformation; that is, it produces [the elements] specifically. From that which is thus impelled, space (ākāśa) is born. Of that space, there exists a quality called sound (śabda). A quality is said to be dependent, and space is its substratum. For indeed, without space, the existence of sound is impossible. (1.75)
From ether, undergoing transformation, there arises the pure and powerful wind, which carries all fragrances; it is indeed considered to have the quality of touch.

The arising of one element from another element is not accepted here, because it is admitted that all elements arise from the *mahat* (the Great Principle). Therefore, it is explained as follows: immediately after space (*ākāśa*), from the *mahat* undergoing transformation and having attained the state of the subtle element of touch (*sparśamātra*), wind (*vāyu*) is born. It carries all odors, both pure and impure; moreover, it is itself pure and purifying. It is powerful. Whatever modification exists in the form of motion, characterized by trembling, throwing, moving upward, downward, or horizontally—that is the activity of wind. To demonstrate that whatever is moved or vibrated is entirely dependent upon wind, it is said to be "powerful. Furthermore, the ablative cases (*pañcamī*) used in the subsequent verses do not imply a sense of being produced; rather, they should be construed as meaning "immediately after wind" and so forth. (1.76)
From fire as well, undergoing transformation, there arises luminous light that dispels darkness; it is said to possess the quality of form. 1.77

By the two words "virociṣṇu" (shining) and "bhāsvat" (radiant), which have the same meaning, its self-illuminating and other-illuminating nature is established: it is itself luminous and it illuminates others. (1.77)
And from light, undergoing transformation, water is said to arise with the quality of taste;
from water, earth arises with the quality of smell—such is the creation from the beginning.

Taste, beginning with sweet, is a quality of water; smell, both fragrant and foul, is a quality of earth. Thus say the Vaiśeṣikas: "Smell exists only in earth" (Praśastapādabhāṣya 4.1). These are the inherent qualities of each element, though they become intermingled through combination. As it has been said: "Whichever [element] is the *n*-th [in the sequence]... (Manusmṛti 1.20). This enumeration of qualities is useful for the contemplation of the self (*adhyātmacintā*). For it was stated by the author of the Purāṇa: "Those who contemplate the senses remain here for ten *manvantaras*."
But the elemental beings number a full hundred, while those possessed of self-consciousness number a thousand.
Ten thousand high-souled ones who contemplate the ego remain free from fever;
but one hundred thousand remain as those who contemplate the unmanifest.
Having attained the Person who is devoid of qualities, no further enumeration exists.
That divine age (*yuga*) which was previously stated to consist of twelve thousand [years], multiplied by seventy-one, is here called a *manvantara*. (1.79)
Seventy-one divine yugas constitute a period of time called a manvantara.
The Supreme Lord, as if in play, repeatedly brings about innumerable Manvantaras, as well as creation and dissolution. 1.80.

"‘Incalculable’ (asaṃkhyāni) means that no such number exists. But is it not heard in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* and other sciences that there are fourteen *manvantaras*? It is said in reply: they are indeed incalculable because of their repetition, just as the twelve months [are repeated in every year]. Furthermore, the repetition of creation and dissolution is truly unceasing. [The text says] "He does this as if playing"; play arises from a desire for pleasure. Since He has all His desires fulfilled and consists solely of bliss, creation and dissolution are not prompted by play. It is for this very reason that the word "as if" (*iva*) is employed. Regarding this, the solution has already been stated previously: the knowers of Brahman maintain that even in the world, the activity of kings and others is seen to proceed both from play (*līlayā*) and from curiosity (*kautukena*). (1.80)
In the Kṛta age, the Dharma was complete with its four quarters, as was Truth;
no acquisition whatsoever occurred through unrighteousness among human beings.

That which has four feet (*catuṣpād*) is *dharma*. Since sacrifice and the like constitute *dharma*, and since its nature is that of something to be performed, it lacks a physical body; therefore, the word "foot" (*pāda*) here does not denote a limb of a body. What then? It denotes a mere portion. For *dharma* has no body, whether human-shaped or animal-like, such as that of a beast or a bird. Thus, being endowed with its own four parts, it is called "four-footed. Consequently, this *dharma*, in its entirety consisting of four parts, existed during the Kṛta Age. To begin with, regarding sacrifice, when it is in the state of performance, there are four officiating priests (*hotṛka*): the Hotṛ, the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, and the Adhvaryu. Alternatively, the four castes (*varṇa*) or the stages of life (*āśrama*) are the performers. In any case, whatever *dharma* is declared in the Veda, all of it was practiced at that time without even a partial deficiency; it was performed in its entirety, free from defects. The number four is used here by way of predominance. This should be applied similarly to giving and other duties: the giver, the object, the recipient, and the purity of intention. Or else, [the four parts are] sacrifice, giving, austerity, and knowledge—as he will say later: "Tolerance is supreme" (MDh 1.86).

Alternatively, *dharma* is the sentence that sets forth the *dharma*. And it has four feet (*pāda*), which are the four classes of words: nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*). Thus it is said: "Four are the measured steps of speech; those Brahmins who are wise know them" (RV 1.164.45ab). "Wise" means those who have mastery over their minds, who are capable, learned, and righteous. But nowadays:
"The three that are hidden in the cave do not stir;
for they do not shine forth. Humans speak only the fourth part of speech. (RV 1.164.45)

Human beings say that a fourth part [of the Veda] has been lost. This is what is meant: originally, no Vedic statement was separated [from its source], nor was there any division of Vedic recensions (*śākhā*); but nowadays, much has been separated.

And "all this is indeed truth" is the connection [to be supplied]. Although truth is included within *dharma* because it is enjoined as such, it is taught separately for the sake of emphasizing its primacy, or else for the sake of indicating its causal function. Truth is the cause of the entire performance of *dharma*. Those who are untruthful, however, perform some actions and abandon others merely for the sake of winning over the world.

Through unrighteousness—that is, by a prohibited path—no sacred knowledge (*āgama*), learning (*vidyā*), or wealth accrues (*upavartate*) to the practitioner; this is due to the inherent nature of the age (*yugasvābhāvya*). Men do not acquire knowledge through unrighteousness, nor do they earn wealth. Since knowledge and wealth are the causes for the practice of dharma, their purity is stated here as the cause for the existence of all dharma. (1.81)
In the other [ages], Dharma exists by means of tradition (āgama), but it has been reduced by one quarter; through theft, falsehood, and deceit, Dharma likewise departs quarter by quarter. (1.82)

In the ages other than the Kṛtayuga, Dharma declined quarter by quarter from that which was known as the Veda; in each successive age, it was diminished and removed, one quarter at a time. The branches of the Veda became lost due to the deficiency in men’s power of comprehension and retention.
