Even that Dharma currently practiced today, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and others, is likewise falling away quarter by quarter through theft and other such faults. Because the officiating priests, the sacrificers, the donors, and the recipients are possessed of these defects, Dharma is not accomplished according to the prescribed rule. Consequently, the fruit as described is not obtained. Therefore, there is no correspondence between the ages and the causes of the decline of Dharma—such as theft and the like—in their respective order, because all of these [faults] are observed today. (1.82)
In the Kṛta age, they are free from disease, have all their aims accomplished, and live for four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one quarter at each stage.

They are free from disease because of the absence of unrighteousness (*adharma*), which is the cause of disease; "disease" means illness. All four castes have their desired objects accomplished. "Object" (*artha*) means purpose. Alternatively, all the objects of those rites performed for specific desires are accomplished; because there is no obstruction, the attainment of the entire fruit occurs without hindrance. Thus, they have a lifespan of four hundred years.

But is it not heard in the science of longevity (*āyurveda*) that "He lived for one hundred and sixteen years" (ChU 3.16.7)? For this very reason, they say: the word "hundred years" here indicates a stage of life; [the meaning is] "they live through four stages of life," meaning they do not die before their full lifespan, nor do they die without reaching the fourth stage. For this reason, he says in the second half-verse that "life wanes. Since the increase of life was mentioned previously, it is logical that its decrease is stated subsequently. Regarding the term "pādaśaḥ": here, a "quarter" (*pāda*) does not mean a fourth part, but rather a mere portion. The meaning is that life is diminished by degrees. Thus, some die as children, some as youths, and some having reached old age. A full lifespan is difficult to obtain. (1.83)
The lifespan ordained for mortals by the Vedas, as well as the fruits of their ritual actions and the powers of embodied beings, bear fruit in the world according to the age. 1.84.

Some say: the lifespan prescribed in the Vedas, such as that required for rituals lasting a thousand years and so forth, bears fruit according to the age (*yuga*); it is realized in accordance with the specific age, not in all ages alike. Nowadays, no one lives for a thousand years; whoever lives a long life at all lives for a hundred years.

Others do not respect that [interpretation], because in long-duration sacrificial sessions (*dīrghasattra*), the word *saṃvatsara* is established as referring to days (cf. PMS 6.7.31–40), since otherwise there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the contradiction with another injunction. For the text there reads: "Fifty-five threefold years," and so forth. In that context, three days are already established by virtue of the *Gavāmayana* being the archetype; however, the specific number "fifty-five" is an injunction because it was not previously established. If a further state of being a "year" were perceived, the sentence would be split. Therefore, one of the two must necessarily be accepted as a restatement (*anuvāda*). Since the word *saṃvatsara*—referring to a collection of three hundred and sixty days—is seen to be used elsewhere without distinction for a period consisting of solar, civil, or other measures, it is appropriate to accept it as a restatement of those days through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Others, however, argue that in the *mantra* and *arthavāda* passages—such as "O gods, there are indeed a hundred autumns before us" (*RV* 1.89.9) and "Man has a lifespan of a hundred years" (*KS* 34.5)—the word "hundred" (*śata*) is listed among the names for "many," and "muchness" (*bahutva*) is not fixed; for according to the [character of the] age (*yuga*), people may be long-lived or short-lived. If one were to explain it literally, then in the *kali* age everyone would have a lifespan of exactly a hundred years. Alternatively, regarding those rites performed by one desiring long life, no specific measure is heard in the scripture; in such cases, the measure must be understood according to the respective age.

Blessings (*āśiṣaḥ*): other Vedic injunctions concerning results as well; [the fruits] of optional rites (*kāmyānāṃ karmaṇām*). Although longevity (*āyuṣ*) is also a desired object, it is taught separately because of its preeminence. For thus it is said: "Longevity is indeed the supreme desire. "Power" (*prabhāvaḥ*) means extraordinary capacity, the possession of qualities such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth, the power of cursing, and the granting of boons. The phrase "yielding fruit according to the age" (*anuyugaṃ phalanti*) is to be applied in every case. 1.84.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are one way, those in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages are different,
and those in the Kali age are yet another, according to the decline of the respective ages.

This is the conclusion regarding the difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things due to the difference in time, as previously stated. The word *dharma* does not refer exclusively to sacrifices and the like; rather, it applies to the mere qualities of things. Other qualities of things arise according to each age (*yuga*), as was shown earlier. Just as the nature of things is one in spring, another in summer, and yet another in the rainy season, so it is also with respect to the ages. Furthermore, this "otherness" here does not mean that causes abandon their observed effects to produce different effects; rather, it is because of a diminution of power (*śakti*) resulting in the production of an incomplete effect. Thus he says: "in accordance with the decline of the ages. "Decline" (*hrāsa*) means deficiency (*nyūnatā*). (1.85)
Austerity is said to be supreme in the Kṛta age, knowledge in the Tretā;
they say sacrifice alone is the path in the Dvāpara, and charity alone in the Kali age.

This other distinction regarding the nature of the *yugas* is now described. Since there is no injunction in the Veda for *tapas* (austerity) and the other virtues according to the specific divisions of the *yugas*, all of them must be practiced at all times. This [verse], however, being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), must be explained in some way or another. For it is described thus in the *Itihāsas*: austerity is primary, and it yields great fruit; those who are long-lived and free from disease are capable of austerity. With this intention it is said. Knowledge here refers to that concerning the inner self (*adhyātma*); because of the bodily affliction [involved], internal restraint is not excessively difficult. But in sacrifice (*yajña*), there is great physical hardship; therefore, in the *Dvāpara* age, sacrifice is primary. As for charity (*dāna*), there is no bodily affliction, no internal restraint, and it does not require excessive learning; thus its ease of accomplishment is emphasized. (1.86)
But for the sake of protecting this entire creation, that one of great splendor assigned distinct duties to those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.

The division of time has been explained. Now the qualities of the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes are described. This is the introduction: for the sake of the preservation and protection of the entire creation and all the worlds, the Greatly Resplendent Prajāpati ordained and established the duties—concerned with both visible and invisible ends—for the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who were born from his mouth and the other [limbs]. (1.87)
Now those actions are being described. 1.88.
He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, as well as giving gifts and receiving them. (1.88)
The protection of subjects, giving, sacrifice, study, and lack of attachment to sense-objects: this, in brief, is the duty of a Kṣatriya. [1.89]
Objects (*viṣaya*) are said to be things such as the sounds of songs that give rise to longing; "non-attachment" (*aprasaṅga*) therein means not indulging in them again and again. (1.89)
The protection of cattle, giving, sacrifice, study, trade, moneylending, and agriculture are the duties of the Vaiśya. (1.90)

Trade (*vanikpatha*) is the acquisition of wealth through commercial activities via land routes, water routes, and so forth; it is the bringing together of goods from other regions for use by a king in whose realm one resides. Lending at interest (*kusīda*) is the investment of wealth for the sake of profit. || 1.90 ||
But the Lord ordained only one duty for the Śūdra: to serve these very castes without malice. (1.91)

The Lord Prajāpati prescribed one single duty for the Śūdra: "Service to these—namely the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—must be performed by you without envy and without censure; even in thought, no resentment toward them should be harbored. Service (*śuśrūṣā*) means attendance, performing tasks conducive to their welfare, such as massaging their bodies, and following their will. This is the visible purpose for the Śūdra. Furthermore, because it is a singular injunction, acts such as giving gifts are not thereby prohibited. The specific injunction regarding these duties will follow later; therefore, we shall demonstrate there itself the distinct nature of sacrifices and other rites. (1.91)
The human being is proclaimed to be more pure above the navel;
therefore, his mouth was declared by the Self-Existent One to be the most pure of all.

A human being is pure down to the ends of the feet; his body is even more pure above the navel, and the face is the purest of all. And this was stated by the Puruṣa himself, the cause of the world, [in the following verse]: 1.92.

What follows from this? To this he says: "Because of his birth from the highest limb, because of his seniority, and because he upholds the Veda, the Brāhmaṇa is by right the lord of this entire creation. (1.93)

The "head" (*uttamāṅga*) is the crown of the head. From that [head] arises—the birth of the Brāhmaṇa. He is the "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) because he was created by Brahmā prior to the other castes, due to his being the bearer of the *brahman*, i.e., the Veda; for that [Vedic knowledge] is prescribed for him with particular distinction. Therefore, for all the world, on account of these three reasons, the Brāhmaṇa is a "lord" (*prabhu*), as it were. A lord is one who should be approached with humility, and one must abide by his command in accordance with *dharma*. "A lord by virtue of *dharma*" means a lord in respect to *dharma*. The suffix *-tasi* is used here according to the rule beginning with "ādyādi. (1.93)

For the Self-Existent One himself, having performed austerities, first created him from his own mouth for the purpose of conveying the offerings to the gods and ancestors, and for the protection of this entire world.

This is for the purpose of specifying the three aforementioned reasons. Furthermore, the head is the preeminent limb even for any other person; moreover, the Self-existent One (Svayaṃbhū) created that Brāhmaṇa from his own mouth. And this birth from the head occurred after he had performed austerity (*tapas*). He states [the Brāhmaṇa’s] primacy by saying "from the beginning. That which is performed with reference to the gods is *havya* (an oblation), and that which is performed with reference to the ancestors is *kavya* (an offering). For the purpose of conveying these two—that is, for the sake of delivering them to the gods and the ancestors—one must somehow interpret the gerundive (*kṛtya*) in *abhivāhyāya* as denoting an abstract state (*bhāve*), since the root *vah* (to carry) is transitive. And by means of that function, there is the protection and preservation of the entire triple world. The gods subsist on what is offered from here [by humans]. And they, in turn, ripen and cause the plants to ripen through cold, heat, and rain. Thus, protection arises from mutual assistance. (1.94)
What being is greater than he, whose mouth the denizens of heaven always consume as sacrificial offerings (havya), and the ancestors likewise consume as ancestral offerings (kavya)? 1.95.

This demonstrates what was previously stated regarding the carrying of oblations (*havya*) and so forth. Those whose abode or home is the third heaven (*tridiva*) are thus called; they are the gods dwelling in heaven. The gods attend upon the food eaten by a Brāhmaṇa. In the *śrāddha* rite, the feeding of Brāhmaṇas is prescribed for the sake of the Viśvedevas as a constituent part of the ancestral (*pitrya*) ritual. It is with reference to that [feeding] that this is said. What else could be more significant, superior, or excellent than that? This is forgotten by the author himself. Since the gods and ancestors occupy the highest and middle stations and are imperceptible, they have no other means of obtaining food except through the feeding of Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is great. (1.95)
Among beings, those endowed with breath are the best; among those endowed with breath, those who live by their intelligence are superior;
among the intelligent, men are the best; and among men, the Brāhmaṇas are traditionally held to be the most excellent.

Those entities on earth—whether stationary, such as trees and the like, or moving, such as worms and insects—are designated by the term *bhūta*. Among them, those living beings capable of activities such as eating and moving about are superior [143], for they experience pleasure more acutely. Among them, those who live by means of intelligence, discriminating between what is beneficial and what is harmful—such as dogs and jackals—are superior; for when tormented by heat, they seek shade, and when afflicted by cold, they seek sunlight, and they abandon a place where there is no food. Superior to these are human beings, and among them, the Brāhmaṇas. For they are most worthy of honor in the world and are not treated with contempt by anyone; indeed, for their killing, there is a great penance based solely on their caste [1.96].

Among the Brahmins, those who are learned; among the learned, those whose intellects are refined; among those of refined intellect, those who perform their duties; and among those who perform their duties, those who know Brahman.

The preeminence of the learned (*vidvas*) arises from their eligibility for sacrifices and other rites that yield great fruits. Among them, those of perfected intellect (*kṛtabuddhi*)—who have fully realized the true meaning of the Vedas—are not defiled by the Buddhists and others. Even among them, there are performers of actions, who are practitioners of rituals; for they are not harmed by performing what is enjoined and avoiding what is prohibited. Among them, too, there are knowers of Brahman (*brahmavedin*), because of their identity with the nature of Brahman; for therein lies imperishable bliss. (1.97)
When the specific qualities of a Brāhmaṇa—such as learning and the like—have been shown, someone might despise a Brāhmaṇa who possesses only his caste. To prevent this, the following is said:
The very birth of a Brāhmaṇa is the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
for he is born for the sake of Dharma and is fit for becoming Brahman. (1.98)

"Birth alone," meaning the very arising, "having abandoned qualities"—that is, birth itself; for a Brāhmaṇa, "caste alone" is the eternal embodiment, the body, of Dharma. One who has been born for the sake of Dharma and consecrated by the second birth, namely the initiation (upanayana)—for that birth for the sake of Dharma leads to, or results in, the state of Brahmanhood. This is a praise [stating]: "Having cast off the body of Dharma, one becomes a partaker of supreme bliss. (1.98)
For when a Brāhmaṇa is born, he is indeed born preeminent upon the earth;
he is the lord of all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma.

He stands above the entire world; by the term "superiority" (*śraiṣṭhya*), he expresses his state of being on high. By the phrase "lord of all beings," he expresses his sovereignty (*prabhutva*). He is born for the protection of the treasury known as Dharma. A treasury (*kośa*) is an accumulation of material goods; by way of analogy, the accumulation of Dharma is called a treasury. (1.99)
"Everything that exists within the world belongs to the Brāhmaṇa as his own;
by virtue of his preeminence and noble birth, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this. (1.100)

Fearing that one who is not content might engage again in receiving gifts and the like, which would constitute a misdeed, he offers this resolution: "All this wealth existing within the three worlds is the property of the Brāhmaṇa; herein no 'receiving' exists. He takes it by virtue of his lordship, not as a recipient. This is a statement of praise, not an injunction; for this very reason, the word *arhati* (he deserves) is used. *Abhijana* means the excellence of noble birth. (1.100)
The Brāhmaṇa eats only his own, wears his own, and gives away his own; it is through the Brāhmaṇa’s compassion that other people eat at all. 1.101.

That which he eats in another’s house in the form of hospitality and so forth is indeed his own; one should not think, "This is through another's cooking. He wears [clothing]—whether he obtains a garment by begging or without begging—it is not for the sake of acquisition, but rather for the application of his own [body] to clothing. Let alone what he takes for his own use, even that which is abundant therein and what he gives to others, though belonging to another, is not improper for him. Compassion (*ānṛśaṃsya*) is mercy. By virtue of his great-souled nature (*mahāsattvatā*), kings upon the earth utilize their own wealth. Otherwise, if he were to wish, "Having taken this, I shall apply it to my own purposes," then everyone would become destitute and useless. (1.101)
For the sake of discerning his [the king's] duties, as well as those of the others in their proper order, the wise Svāyambhuva Manu composed this treatise. (1.102)

This verse is intended to demonstrate the fruit of the entire praise of the Brāhmaṇa. This treatise, which possesses such great purpose, was composed for the sake of discerning the duties of that Brāhmaṇa—who is most exalted by his own ultimate greatness—to distinguish between actions, namely: "these actions are to be performed" and "these are to be avoided. Furthermore, it was fashioned—that is, created—for the remaining castes, beginning with the Kṣatriyas, in their proper order; primarily for the Brāhmaṇa, and by extension for the Kṣatriyas and others. (1.102)
This should be studied with diligence by a learned Brahmin and correctly expounded to his disciples; it must not be taught by anyone else. 1.103.

"It should be studied and it should be expounded"—this *kṛtya* suffix denotes fitness (*arhe*), not an injunction (*vidhau*). From the second chapter onwards, the treatise (*śāstra*) will proceed; for this first chapter is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). There is no injunction here at all. Therefore, just as in the statement "The rice is fit for the King's meal," which is a praise of the rice and does not imply a prohibition of others from eating it, so too here there is no prohibition that it must not be studied or expounded by anyone else; rather, it is solely a praise of the treatise. The Brāhmaṇa is the most excellent in the entire world, and this is the treatise among all treatises; therefore, it is worthy of being studied and expounded by such a learned Brāhmaṇa, and it cannot be studied or expounded by everyone indiscriminately. For this very reason, he says "with effort" (*prayatnataḥ*). As long as great effort is not applied, and as long as the self is not refined through other sciences such as logic (*tarka*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and hermeneutics (*mīmāṃsā*), it is not possible to expound this. Consequently, by "study" (*adhyayana*), "listening" (*śravaṇa*) is indicated; for it is learning that is useful for scholarship, not mere rote recitation. Indeed, if study were an injunction, scholarship would have to be regarded as its transcendental result (*adṛṣṭa*), and it is not proper to say, "In an injunction, listening is indicated by study. It is not appropriate for a thing enjoined to serve as a mere indicator (*lakṣaṇārthatā*). However, in an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), a figurative description (*guṇavāda*) following another means of knowledge is not a fault. Therefore, the treatise has the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) as its qualified audience. This will be explained specifically later on. (1.103)
A Brahmin who studies this treatise and whose vows are well-proclaimed is never defiled by the faults of action born of mind, speech, or body. (1.104)

Having thus praised the scripture by way of its connection to the purpose of the Brahmin, he now praises it directly: one who knows this scripture becomes "one whose vows are praised," meaning one who becomes a performer of the complete observance of restraints (*yama*) and disciplines (*niyama*). Knowing from the scripture that there is transgression (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform [these duties], one practices them all out of fear of that [transgression], according to the scripture. While practicing, one is not smeared—that is, not bound—by the defects produced by the transgression of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited. (1.104)
He purifies his lineage, seven ancestors and seven descendants;
indeed, even he alone is worthy of this entire earth. (1.105)

He becomes a sanctifier of the assembly. A "line" (*paṅkti*) is said to be a group arranged in a specific sequence; he purifies it, that is, makes it stainless. By his presence, all who are wicked become non-wicked. He is worthy of receiving the earth bounded by the oceans—seven ancestors above, born of his own lineage such as his father and so forth, and seven descendants below, those yet to be born. For knowledge of the Dharma is the cause for the authority to receive gifts; indeed, from this [knowledge] all dharmas are known. (1.105)
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect; this constantly brings renown; this is the supreme state of ultimate bliss. 1.106

*Svasti* is the non-destruction of a desired object. *Ayana* means reaching or attaining. That by which *svasti* is attained is *svastyayana*. It is the most excellent (*śreṣṭha*) among other practices such as recitation (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*), for their performance is not possible without a treatise (*śāstra*); therefore, because it is the cause for their performance, this [treatise] is the most excellent. Alternatively, the very sentences that convey the knowledge of Dharma are superior, whereas actual performance is laborious; hence it is called "the most excellent. This increases the intellect (*buddhivivardhana*). For when a treatise is studied, the increase of the intellect is well-known, arising from the illumination of its meaning and the loosening of mental knots. This is conducive to fame (*yaśasya*); one who knows the Dharma gains renown when questioned by those in doubt. That which is the cause of fame is *yaśasya*. Fame is the renown resulting from qualities such as learning and magnanimity. It is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), because it is the cause of the knowledge of action and wisdom that lead to the attainment of pleasure unmingled with suffering—characterized as heaven and liberation—and thus it is the highest excellence. (1.106)
In this Dharma, the merits and defects of actions have been declared in their entirety, as well as the eternal conduct for all four castes. 1.107

Now, he states the independence of his own treatise regarding its subject matter by virtue of its complete treatment thereof: "Whatever duty (dharma) there may be, all that has been declared in this treatise in its entirety. Therefore, for the knowledge of dharma, no dependence on other treatises should be placed [upon them]"—this is a hyperbolic praise (*atiśayokti*). In this treatise, dharma based on the Smṛtis is stated in its entirety, without remainder, as well as the merits and defects of actions. The "merits and defects" of actions such as sacrifices (*yāga*) and the like, or the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and the like, refer to their desirable and undesirable fruits. For completeness consists in this: the essential nature of the action, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the specific fruit, the connection with a specific agent, and the distinction between obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) acts. All of this is promised by the term "merits and defects. When "dharma" is mentioned, the inclusion of the word "actions" (*karman*) is for the purpose of completing the meter. "Of all four castes"—this too is for the sake of completeness; whoever is entitled to dharma, for all of them, the acquisition of dharma comes from this source. "And also eternal conduct (*ācāra*)"—conduct which is the authority for dharma is here called "conduct. We shall examine this further in the second chapter. "Eternal" means established through an unbroken tradition of elders, not something initiated by people of the present day. (1.107)
Conduct is the supreme dharma, as declared in the Śruti and in the Smṛti;
therefore, a self-possessed twice-born man should always be constantly devoted to it. 1.108

The supreme, most excellent dharma is the practice (ācāra) as declared in the Śruti, that is, the Veda; and the Smārta, that which is declared in the Smṛtis. Therefore, one who possesses self-control (ātmavān), desiring his own welfare, should be constantly engaged in this dharma of practice; he should perform it perpetually. Since every person has a self, the possessive suffix -mat is used here to express the sense of "one who has that" (taddhitaparatva). (1.108)
A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Vedas;
however, one who is endowed with right conduct shall partake of the full fruit. 1.109

This is another way of praising right conduct (*ācāra*). One who has fallen away from right conduct, being devoid of right conduct, does not obtain the fruit of the Vedas. It has been stated that the "fruit of the Vedas" is the fruit resulting from the performance of rites prescribed by the Vedas. This is a censure: even if one performs all Vedic rites in their entirety and without deficiency, if one is fallen from right conduct, one does not enjoy the fruits such as the desire for a son and so forth. This same point is expressed by way of its opposite: "But one joined with right conduct obtains the full fruit of optional rites. Regarding this, some say: "Because of the word 'full,' there is still a connection with the fruit of optional rites for one devoid of right conduct, though not the attainment of the entire fruit. That is of no consequence, because this is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). 1.109.
Thus, having observed through conduct the course of Dharma, the sages took up conduct as the supreme root of all austerity. 1.110

Whatever austerity there may be—whether breath control, silence, restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), the *kṛcchra* penance, the *cāndrāyaṇa*, fasting, and so forth—the root for the production of the fruit of all that is right conduct (*ācāra*). Therefore, sages seeking the fruit of austerity have accepted, or taken, that very conduct as the root, as the cause. For by observing conduct, the sages perceive the course, or attainment, of Dharma; thus says the Śruti: "Even though austerity causes great hardship, it does not bear fruit for one devoid of conduct. (1.110)
And [he taught] the origin of the world, the very procedure for the formative factors (saṃskāra),
the practice and observance of vows, and the supreme rite of ritual bathing.

The topics [of dharma] have been stated here; however, for the sake of engaging the listener, the infinite fruit of dharma has been declared by such passages as, "But these are the limits... (MDh 1.50). Fearing that people might become despondent—thinking, "This is beyond the senses, infinite, and difficult to cross"—the author recites a table of contents (*anukramaṇī*) consisting of a summary of the meaning of the treatise, so as to generate enthusiasm: "The subjects here are only this many, not too many; they can be understood by men who possess faith. Thus, a path taught in brief becomes easier to traverse when it is stepped upon.

The origin of the world—meaning the measurement of time, the differentiation of the nature of reality, the praise of the Brāhmaṇas, and so forth—is all included within the account of the world's origin. This is stated as an *arthavāda* (explanatory or commendatory statement) and not as a primary object of knowledge (*prameya*). [It also includes] the injunctions for purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and the performance of vows and observances. The purificatory rites are those beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*); their "injunction" (*vidhi*) is the necessity of performing them. The "performance of vows and observances" (*vratacaryopacāra*) refers to the conduct or the procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) of the student (*brahmacārin*). These constitute the subject matter of the second chapter. "Bathing" (*snāna*) is a specific purificatory rite for one returning from the teacher’s house. (1.111)
The acquisition of a wife, the characteristics of marriages, the procedure for the great sacrifices, and the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha). || 1.112 ||

The "attainment of wives" refers to the taking of a spouse; the "characteristics" of the various marriages, such as the *brāhma* and others, as well as the means for obtaining them, serve as the cause for understanding their essential nature. The "great sacrifices" (*mahāyajña*) are the five, beginning with the *vaiśvadeva*. The "ritual procedure" (*kalpa*) for the *śrāddha*, which is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), refers to its rules and the manner of performance. The inclusion of the terms "paragrahaṇa" and "śāśvatagrahaṇa" is for the purpose of completing the meter. This is the subject matter of the third chapter. (1.112)
The characteristics of the modes of livelihood, the vows of a Snātaka, the edible and non-edible, ritual purity, and the purification of substances. (1.113)
The application of the duties of women, asceticism, liberation, and renunciation itself;
the entire duty of kings and the determination of legal cases.
The rules for questioning witnesses, the law concerning husband and wife,
the law of partition, gambling, and the removal of social thorns.
[He described] the conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the origin of the mixed castes, the duties of the social orders in times of distress, and likewise the rules for expiation.

The characteristics of the modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*)—the means of subsistence consisting of the acquisition of wealth, such as service and so forth; the observances (*vrata*) for a *snātaka* who has completed his Vedic studies and returned from the teacher’s house, such as "one should not look at the rising sun" (MDh 4.37); the fourth topic consists of these. The distinction between what is fit and unfit to be eaten—such as "five five-nailed animals are edible" and "onions and the like are inedible"; purity (*śauca*), both that pertaining to time, such as at birth and so forth, and the purification of substances by water and other means; and the application of duties for women, including their relations [to the husband] as a girl, a young woman, and so forth—this constitutes the fifth book.

*Tāpasya* is that which is beneficial for an ascetic (*tāpasa*). An ascetic is one whose primary practice is austerity (*tapas*), namely a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); his duty is *tāpasya*. Liberation (*mokṣa*) is the duty of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), and renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is indeed a specific form of that; this will be demonstrated in that very [section]. This, however, is the subject matter of the sixth chapter.
The entire duty of a king—who is authorized to protect the earth and has attained sovereignty, whether having visible results or invisible results—is the scope of the seventh chapter.

The "determination of legal matters" (*kāryāṇāṃ vinirṇayaḥ*) refers to the ascertainment of debts and other such cases through investigation and the removal of doubt; it is the resolution regarding what must be performed. As for the "rule regarding the examination of witnesses," this is mentioned separately because of its preeminence. This subject matter constitutes the eighth book.

The *dharma* of husband and wife refers to their mutual conduct when staying in one place or when separated by travel. The *dharma* of partitioning inheritance; gambling—the rule concerning that is expressed by the word "gambling"; and the clearing away of thorns, such as thieves and forest-dwellers, which are the means for expelling them from the kingdom. Although [the topics of] partition and so forth need not be mentioned separately—since they are included within the eighteen titles of law (*padāni*) by the very phrase "and of legal matters"—they are mentioned separately here because of the division of the chapters. The conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras is the performance of their own duties; this is treated in the ninth [chapter].

The origin—that is, the birth—of those of mixed castes, such as the Kṣattṛ, the Vaidehaka, and others; and the law for times of distress (āpaddharma), which is the duty pertaining to those who have lost their livelihood in a life-threatening emergency: these are treated in the tenth [chapter].
The rules for expiation (prāyaścitta) are in the eleventh. 1.113–6.
The journey through saṃsāra, which arises from the threefold karma;
the supreme good resulting from actions; and the examination of the merits and defects of those actions. || 1.117 ||

The going to *saṃsāra*. A substratum (*dharmī*) is characterized by its attributes (*dharma*). The transmigrating person is the *ātman*; his "going" is the attainment of another body after leaving the present one. Alternatively, the worlds such as the earth, which are the objects of *saṃsāra*, are so called; the "going" therein is as previously described. It is threefold—superior, inferior, and middling—arising from *karman* and caused by auspicious and inauspicious actions. Not only are the destinies said to be caused by *karman*, but also that means for attaining *niḥśreyasa* (the supreme good), beyond which there is no other higher good, namely knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātmajñāna*), has been explained. Furthermore, there is the examination of the merits and defects of prescribed and prohibited actions. 1.117
In this treatise, Manu has declared the eternal laws of regions, the laws of castes, the laws of families, and the laws of heretical sects and guilds. (1.118)

This very point confirms the statement of completeness: those ten duties (*daśadharma*) are not to be performed everywhere on the entire earth, but rather in specific localities. Duties based on caste (*jātidharma*) depend on castes such as the Brāhmaṇa and others. Family duties (*kuladharma*) are those established by renowned lineages. Heretical duties (*pāṣaṇḍadharma*) are the practices of prohibited observances based on external traditions (*bāhyasmṛti*); regarding these, it is said: "Heretics (*pāṣaṇḍinaḥ*) are those who persist in improper actions" (MDh 4.30). A "group" (*gaṇa*) is a corporation (*saṃghāta*) of merchants, artisans, actors, and so forth. The Blessed Manu has declared all these duties in this treatise. (1.118)
Just as Manu formerly spoke this scripture when questioned by me, so too do you now learn it from me. 1.119
Awakening is for the purpose of focused attention. 1.119.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu;
thus [ends] the *Manubhāṣya* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi.
